research.topic: State of Zig in 2026 for a native-desktop framework (Zig core + TS runtime + native widgets)
key_findings: Zig 0.16.0 shipped April 13, 2026; its centerpiece is std.Io, a unified I/O interface where every blocking operation takes an explicit `Io` parameter, eliminating function coloring and letting you swap threaded vs event-driven backends without rewriting call sites (per the official 0.16.0 release notes at ziglang.org/download/0.16.0/release-notes.html).

The only production-usable std.Io backend in 0.16 is std.Io.Threaded (thread pool); std.Io.Evented (io_uring on Linux, kqueue on BSD/macOS, Grand Central Dispatch on macOS) landed February 2026 as experimental and the core team explicitly says it needs substantial follow-up before reliable use.

std.Io ships useful concurrency primitives out of the box: Future(T), Group (await/cancel many tasks together), Batch, Select, and cancellation baked into every cancelable operation's error set as error.Canceled — a solid foundation for a framework event/task layer.

'Writergate' (0.15.1, Aug 2025) replaced the generic Reader/Writer with non-generic std.Io.Reader/std.Io.Writer holding caller-provided buffers and requiring explicit .flush(); 0.16 removed the old interfaces entirely, so virtually all pre-2025 Zig I/O code and tutorials are broken on current Zig.

@cImport has been deleted from the language in 0.16: C translation now happens in the build system via b.addTranslateC() and the official `translate-c` package (codeberg.org/ziglang/translate-c), which is the same implementation with more configuration options; std.Build.Step.TranslateC itself is deprecated in favor of that package dependency.

Comptime binding generation is proven for exactly our target toolkits: ianprime0509/zig-gobject generates zero-cost GTK4/GObject bindings from GObject-introspection GIR (tested on Zig 0.15 and master, with comptime-typed signal connection), and mitchellh/zig-objc provides comptime Objective-C runtime bindings (find/subclass classes, add methods, blocks) that Ghostty uses for AppKit.

Package management is workable but immature: build.zig.zon with content-hash-addressed URL fetching (hash is the source of truth, URL is just a mirror), no official registry (Zigistry is unofficial), weak transitive-dependency resolution; 0.16 added local package overrides and project-local fetching, and in June 2026 package management moved fully into the build system's maker process.

Cross-compilation remains Zig's superpower: zig cc bundles clang plus libc headers for all targets, glibc version is selectable via target suffix (e.g. x86_64-linux-gnu.2.31), musl gives fully static Linux binaries, and macOS frameworks link via SDKROOT — but a GTK4-linked Linux binary is not hermetic anyway since GTK/GLib are system libraries, so Linux packaging will still want per-distro builds or flatpak.

Breaking-change cadence is the biggest operational risk: Ghostty skipped Zig 0.15 entirely (stayed on 0.14.1 for its 1.2 release) and its 0.16 migration (ghostty-org/ghostty#12228, PR #12726) is still unmerged in July 2026 — three months after 0.16 shipped — even though its dependencies (libxev, zig-objc, libvaxis, z2d) are already ported; the std.Io rework touches everything that does filesystem/thread/timer work and std.posix was almost completely removed.

Bun abandoned Zig: after Anthropic's acquisition, a 1M+ line Rust rewrite was merged May 14, 2026; Bun 1.3.14 was the final Zig-based version (the host's Bun 1.3.13 is on that dying line), motivated by an unmergeable custom Zig compiler fork and Zig's strict no-AI contribution policy (confirmed by The Register, devclass, and the oven-sh/bun repo).

Zig upstream has a hard no-AI-contribution policy, which does not affect agents writing apps in our framework but does mean agent-generated patches can never go upstream to Zig itself, and it signals cultural friction worth knowing about for an agent-first project.

Zig 0.17 is imminent (slipped from June to roughly August 2026 per the ziglang.org devlog): it brings a build-system rework with ~90% faster basic commands via maker/configurer process separation plus LLVM 22 — meaning build.zig APIs will churn again within months of us adopting 0.16.

0.16 also replaced the @Type builtin with eight specialized builtins (@Int, @Struct, @Union, @Enum, @Pointer, @Fn, @Tuple, @EnumLiteral) and added 'juicy main' (std.process.Init parameter giving pre-initialized arena, gpa, io) — both directly relevant to metaprogramming-heavy binding code.

TigerBeetle and Ghostty remain the flagship proofs that large production Zig codebases are viable, and both follow the same discipline: pin one exact Zig version per release, vendor/download that exact toolchain in-repo, and treat each Zig upgrade as a scheduled migration project rather than tracking master.
research.recommendation: Adopt Zig 0.16.0 and pin it exactly (vendored toolchain download or Nix flake input, the Ghostty/TigerBeetle pattern), budgeting one deliberate migration project per Zig release until 1.0; do not track master. Architect all core I/O around the std.Io parameter-passing convention using std.Io.Threaded today so std.Io.Evented becomes a drop-in later, but drive GTK4/AppKit through their own native main loops (GLib main context, NSRunLoop) rather than betting on std.Io event-loop integration. Generate widget bindings with build-system translate-c (the ziglang/translate-c package) for raw headers plus zig-gobject (GTK4, GIR-driven) and mitchellh/zig-objc (AppKit) for idiomatic comptime layers — this stack is proven by Ghostty. Critically, do NOT design around linking Bun's internals as a Zig library: Bun's core is now Rust and its Zig line is dead at 1.3.14, so treat the TypeScript runtime as a clean embedding boundary — either embed a JS engine directly via C API (JavaScriptCore or V8, both battle-tested from Zig) or run Bun/Node as a sidecar process over a fast IPC/FFI bridge that the framework owns. This boundary also keeps the door open for the CEF browser-shell use case.
gotchas: Bun 1.3.x is the end of Bun's Zig lineage (Rust rewrite merged May 2026), so any plan to statically link Bun or reuse its Zig internals (its JSC bindings, event loop) is dead on arrival — design the TS-runtime boundary as engine-agnostic from day one.

Almost all Zig I/O example code, blog posts, and library READMEs from before mid-2025 are broken on 0.15+/0.16 (Writergate plus std.Io); AI agents trained on that corpus will hallucinate removed APIs like std.io.getStdOut().writer(), so the framework's agent docs must include current-idiom Zig snippets.

@cImport no longer exists in 0.16 — C header import requires build.zig wiring (b.addTranslateC / translate-c package), and the translate-c build step historically lacked a clean way to link system libraries (ziglang/zig#20649), which matters for pkg-config-discovered GTK4 flags.

Only std.Io.Threaded is usable in 0.16; std.Io.Evented is explicitly experimental, and nobody has demonstrated integrating std.Io's event loop with the GLib main context or NSRunLoop — keep UI main loops native and bridge with wakeup pipes/dispatch, as Ghostty does with libxev.
Zig 0.17 lands around August 2026 with a build-system rework, so build.zig code written now will need churn within months; keep build logic thin and centralized.

The Zig package manager has no official registry and weak transitive-dependency resolution — pin dependencies by content hash and consider vendoring critical bindings (zig-gobject, zig-objc) to survive upstream breakage.

zig cc's hermetic cross-compilation does not extend to GTK4: Linux builds link system GTK/GLib, so CI needs real per-distro (or containerized) Linux environments; macOS builds need SDKROOT pointing at a real macOS SDK.

Zig's no-AI contribution policy means compiler bugs you hit cannot be fixed upstream by your agents; plan to work around toolchain bugs locally (patched toolchain in the pin) rather than assuming quick upstream fixes.

research.topic: Embedding or integrating Bun (or alternative JS/TS runtimes) with a Zig core in 2026
key_findings: There is no embeddable libbun: the request to expose Bun as a C-compatible library is oven-sh/bun issue #12017 (open since June 2024, assigned to cirospaciari, nothing shipped as of July 2026), and issue #14252 was closed as its duplicate, so Bun today is only consumable as a standalone executable.

Bun was rewritten from Zig to Rust in May 2026 (PR #30412, merged May 14, 2026, roughly one million lines generated largely by Claude Code agents after Anthropic acquired Bun in December 2025); v1.3.14 (released July 8, 2026) is the last stable Zig-lineage release and v1.4.0 will be the first Rust release, which permanently kills any 'link Bun's Zig source into our Zig binary' plan.

Even before the rewrite, source-level integration was impractical: Bun's build mixed CMake, JS scripts, a custom WebKit fork, and a pinned older Zig toolchain (not the host's 0.16.0), Ziggit threads explicitly steered people away from consuming Bun as a Zig dependency, and build.zig has now been deleted from main (404).

bun:ffi (dlopen) calls any C-ABI shared library including Zig-built ones, supports i8-u64/f32/f64/ptr/buffer/cstring plus napi_env/napi_value types, claims 2-6x lower call overhead than Node-API, and embeds TinyCC for JIT-compiling C at runtime, but Bun's own docs still mark it experimental with known bugs and explicitly recommend Node-API modules for production stability.

Bun's Node-API (napi) implementation was fully rewritten with large performance gains (Bun's release notes cite node-sdl becoming ~100x faster), and the Rust rewrite hit 99.8% test compatibility, so a Zig shared library exposing napi symbols is the stable, officially recommended high-frequency native-call path from Bun.

Per-call FFI overhead is real and can exceed the native work being done: an independent benchmark showed a naive Rust-via-bun:ffi function losing to pure TypeScript (1.47ms vs 1.33ms per iteration), so high-frequency UI updates must be batched into binary command buffers (ArrayBuffer) crossed once per frame rather than one FFI call per widget property.

JSCallback lets native code call back into JS with an optional experimental 'threadsafe' mode that costs extra per call and must be explicitly .close()d, and it has open memory-leak reports (e.g. oven-sh/bun#7582); the robust event path is native-to-JS via a napi threadsafe function or a socket/pipe, not JSCallback fan-out.

bun build --compile produces a single-file executable bundling the Bun runtime plus all JS/TS, supports cross-compilation via --target and embedding assets including .node addons, giving a one-binary distribution story if Bun is the host process.

Bun.spawn's ipc option only works between two Bun processes (it uses JSC structuredClone serialization), so a Zig-host-to-Bun-child channel must be a custom length-prefixed protocol over stdio or a unix socket/named pipe; node:worker_threads is implemented and usable in Bun with caveats (no parent IPC access, native addons load from multiple threads only under conditions).

Embedding JavaScriptCore directly from Zig is proven (Jarred Sumner's zig-javascriptcore example; Bun itself did it for 5 years): the C API ships with macOS as JavaScriptCore.framework and on Linux as javascriptcoregtk-6.0 (part of the WebKitGTK stack, pairs naturally with GTK4, usable without any webview), but Windows requires building and shipping WebKit yourself, and raw JSC gives you no TS transpiler, module loader, event loop, timers, or fetch — you would rebuild half a runtime.

quickjs-ng is actively maintained (v0.15.0 released May 21, 2026, ~2-month release cadence, v0.15.0 specifically fixed embedding from other libraries) and is trivially embeddable pure C with no dependencies, but it is interpreter-only, so it suits an in-process plugin-scripting layer rather than the main React application runtime.

There is no maintained Zig binding for V8 in 2026: lightpanda-io/zig-js-runtime was archived March 19, 2026 (V8 wrapper folded into their browser, pinned to Zig 0.14.0) and fubark/zig-v8 is stale; deno_core is a Rust crate with no C API, so using it from Zig requires writing a Rust extern-C shim and adopting the V8 build burden.

Static Hermes remains research-stage in 2026 (not cleanly installable, aimed at React Native) and its JSI interface is a C++ API rather than a stable C ABI; LibJS (Ladybird) has no supported external embedding story — neither is a realistic 2026 option.

For the React-renderer-drives-native-widgets pattern, keeping layout fully native (GTK4/AppKit do their own layout) means the JS side only sends tree mutations and rarely needs synchronous reads, which is what makes an async batched channel (in-process or cross-process) sufficient — this sidesteps the synchronous-measure problem that forced React Native to move from its async bridge to in-process JSI.
research.recommendation: Do not plan on linking Bun into the Zig binary — no libbun exists and the May 2026 Rust rewrite ended the shared-Zig-source dream. Architect instead around a Zig host binary that owns the process and the platform main loop (mandatory for AppKit's main-thread rule and ideal for the built-in automation/screenshot layer, which then works even if the JS runtime hangs), with Bun (pin 1.3.13/1.3.14 now, validate on 1.4.x Rust when stable) running the React/TSX app. Support two transport modes behind one abstraction: (A) default dev/prod mode — Bun as a child process speaking a length-prefixed binary protocol over a unix socket/named pipe (Bun's built-in ipc is Bun-to-Bun only), with UI mutations batched into per-frame command buffers and events flowing back the same way; (B) an in-process mode where Bun is the host executable and the Zig core is loaded as a Node-API shared library (napi is Bun's stable recommended path; keep bun:ffi only as an experimental fast path) for cases needing synchronous calls. Batching per frame makes either transport fast enough for UI updates since native widgets do their own layout. Reserve quickjs-ng (v0.15.0, actively maintained, pure C) as the future in-process plugin-scripting engine, and treat direct JSC embedding as a fallback only if the Bun dependency becomes untenable (its Windows story requires building WebKit yourself).
gotchas: The 'Rewriting Bun in Rust' blog post reads like satire (11 days, 64 Claude agents, ~$165k in tokens) but is confirmed real by the merged commit and Hacker News threads; expect v1.4.x regressions and pin Bun versions in the framework toolchain.

macOS AppKit requires the process main thread and Bun exposes no event-loop pumping API, so Bun-as-main-process needs fragile run-loop interleaving (pumping NSApp/GTK from JS ticks, as node-gui/yue do); the Zig-host + Bun-child topology avoids this entirely.

bun:ffi is officially experimental with known bugs (including JSCallback memory leaks, issue #7582) and Bun's own docs tell you to use Node-API for anything serious — do not build the core protocol on bun:ffi.

FFI/NAPI per-call overhead can exceed the useful native work; one call per widget-property update will be slower than pure TS — design the renderer around one batched ArrayBuffer command buffer per frame from day one.
Bun.spawn({ipc}) silently only supports Bun-to-Bun peers, so the Zig host cannot use it; you must frame your own protocol over stdio or a socket.

Ecosystem Zig bindings for JS engines are dead or pinned old: lightpanda's zig-js-runtime (archived 2026-03, Zig 0.14.0) and fubark/zig-v8 will not build on the host's Zig 0.16.0 without porting work.
Bun's Zig-era JSC build came from the oven-sh/WebKit fork whose maintenance incentive is unclear post-Rust-rewrite; if you later embed JSC yourself, Windows means building WebKit from source.
JSCallback threadsafe mode adds a per-call penalty and callbacks must be explicitly closed or they leak; prefer napi threadsafe functions or the socket event stream for native-to-JS events.

research.topic: Building a custom React renderer in 2026 (react-reconciler status, host config, React Native Fabric lessons, layout/measurement, Compiler, concurrency)
key_findings: react-reconciler is still officially 'experimental' with no semver guarantees; the latest stable is 0.33.0 (published 2025-10-01, peerDependency react ^19.2.0), with a strict lockstep pairing: 0.31.x <-> React 19.0, 0.32.x <-> 19.1, 0.33.x <-> 19.2, and 0.34.0-canary tracking React canary as of July 2026 (verified via the npm registry).

React 19.2 bumped React's internal reconciler in a way that is NOT backward compatible with 19.1: renderers built on the old host config crash with 'resolveUpdatePriority is not a function' in requestUpdateLane; react-three-fiber v9.5.0 (Dec 2025) solved this by bundling/vendoring the reconciler inside the library, noting 'react-dom already does this', to support all React 19.0-19.2 at once.

React 19-era host config changes (documented in r3f PR #3224): prepareUpdate was removed so diffing moves into commitUpdate (which now receives oldProps and newProps directly); getRootHostContext/getChildHostContext may no longer return null (null now means 'missing context', per facebook/react #25609); getCurrentEventPriority was replaced by resolveUpdatePriority/getCurrentUpdatePriority/setCurrentUpdatePriority; new hooks include maySuspendCommit, waitForCommitToBeReady, shouldAttemptEagerTransition, and trackSchedulerEvent.

The host config has two modes and you must pick one: mutation mode (appendChild/removeChild/commitUpdate style, used by react-dom, classic RN, and ink) and persistent mode (immutable tree cloning, used by RN Fabric); for GTK4/AppKit/Win32 widgets, which are inherently mutable retained trees with add/remove-child APIs, mutation mode is the natural fit.

Production custom renderers to crib from: react-three-fiber v9.5 (mutation mode, React 19.0-19.2, bundled reconciler), ink 6.x (mutation mode + Yoga + per-text-node measure functions; ink 6.7 added React concurrent rendering with synchronized updates and powers Claude Code's TUI), react-nil (a ~100-line null renderer, ideal as a minimal reference and headless test harness), and react-tela (TooTallNate's canvas renderer that runs on the nx.js Switch homebrew runtime, proving react-reconciler works fine in non-Node JS runtimes like Bun).

React Native's New Architecture is now the ONLY architecture: default since RN 0.76, legacy bridge permanently disabled in 0.82 (Oct 2025, newArchEnabled=false is ignored), with legacy code physically deleted through 0.84 (Feb 2026, Hermes V1 default, precompiled iOS binaries) and 0.85 (Apr 2026, shared animation backend, WebAssembly in Hermes) — so Fabric/JSI is the proven, settled design to learn from.

Fabric's pipeline: React renders on the JS thread, commits an immutable C++ ShadowTree, Yoga computes flexbox layout in C++, then a mount phase applies a diffed list of mutation operations on the UI thread — the only thread allowed to touch host views; thread safety comes from immutability (C++ const correctness), and high-priority UI-thread events can run the whole render pipeline synchronously while default renders stay async.

JSI replaced the old async JSON-serialized bridge with synchronous C++ host objects callable directly from the JS engine, which is what enables synchronous measure() and real useLayoutEffect semantics in RN — the key lesson being that the JS<->native boundary needs a synchronous call path for layout reads even if mutations are batched and applied asynchronously.

Copy from Fabric: the retained native-side shadow tree with stable node IDs (this doubles as your automation layer's queryable widget-tree dump), the diffed mount-operation stream applied on the UI thread, and the event-priority mapping (DiscreteEventPriority for clicks/keys, ContinuousEventPriority for scroll/drag, DefaultEventPriority otherwise, exported from react-reconciler/constants).

Skip from Fabric: persistent-mode tree cloning and the Yoga layout engine — RN needs Yoga because iOS/Android views share no layout system, but GTK4 (GtkBox/GtkGrid) and AppKit (NSStackView/Auto Layout) have first-class native layout containers, so the framework can delegate layout to native widgets and avoid reimplementing flexbox; a C++/Zig-side Yoga could be added later only for a custom-drawn widget layer.

Text/layout measurement is entirely the renderer's problem — the host config has no layout: ink attaches a synchronous measure function to each text node that runs inside Yoga's blocking layout pass (handling wrapping, grapheme clusters, CJK double-width, ANSI stripping, in microseconds per node), while Fabric uses a C++ TextLayoutManager that calls platform text APIs; for Bun-driving-Zig this means measurement must go over a synchronous FFI call (bun:ffi is sync), never an async message.

React Compiler 1.0 went stable October 7, 2025 (React Conf); it is a build-time auto-memoization Babel transform that is renderer-agnostic (works on React DOM and React Native alike), so it works with a custom reconciler-based renderer for free and reduces re-render pressure, meaning fewer commits crossing the TS-to-Zig boundary.

Suspense and concurrent features are implemented inside the reconciler, but the renderer must cooperate: implement hideInstance/unhideInstance (and text variants) so Suspense fallbacks can hide committed subtrees without unmounting (for native widgets: gtk_widget_set_visible / NSView.isHidden), implement the update-priority methods so startTransition works, and accept that render-phase host config calls (createInstance, appendInitialChild, etc.) can run multiple times or for trees that are never committed.

The official stance is unchanged in 2026: the react-reconciler README states the host config 'changes very often between releases' and documentation is best-effort, so the practical documentation is the reconciler README plus reading ink and react-three-fiber source.
research.recommendation: Build the TS side on react-reconciler in MUTATION mode running under Bun, and vendor (bundle) an exact react@19.2.x + react-reconciler@0.33.0 pair into the framework exactly as react-three-fiber v9.5 does — never let app developers' React version float against the reconciler. Keep all render-phase host config methods side-effect-free by building lightweight JS-side node descriptors, then at commit time serialize a batched mutation-op list (create/append/remove/update, keyed by monotonically-assigned stable node IDs) over a Bun FFI boundary into the Zig core, which owns the authoritative retained widget tree — that Zig-side tree with stable IDs is simultaneously the mount target, the automation layer's dump-tree source, and the input-synthesis addressing scheme, which is Fabric's shadow-tree idea repurposed. Delegate layout to native containers (GtkBox/NSStackView) instead of porting Yoga, but expose one synchronous FFI entry point for measurement (text and custom widgets) since measure callbacks and useLayoutEffect reads cannot be async. Implement hideInstance/unhideInstance via native visibility toggles and the resolveUpdatePriority family mapped to native event types so Suspense and transitions work from day one, and ship React Compiler 1.0 in the default app template since it is renderer-agnostic and cuts commit traffic across the FFI.
gotchas: react-reconciler does not follow semver and its host config breaks on React MINOR releases (19.1 -> 19.2 broke every unbundled renderer with 'resolveUpdatePriority is not a function'); pinning is not enough — bundle the reconciler into the framework like r3f v9.5 and react-dom do.

Under concurrent rendering, createInstance/appendInitialChild/finalizeInitialChildren can be called for work-in-progress trees that are discarded and never committed; if these allocate real GTK/AppKit widgets you leak native objects — allocate real widgets only at commit, or make render-phase nodes cheap JS descriptors.

prepareUpdate no longer exists in the React 19 host config: commitUpdate must do its own oldProps/newProps diffing, so naive renderers that relied on the precomputed updatePayload silently stop diffing.
getRootHostContext and getChildHostContext must return a non-null value in React 19 (null is now the internal 'missing' marker) — returning null causes confusing crashes far from the actual bug.

Measure functions (Yoga-style) and useLayoutEffect reads are synchronous and blocking; an async IPC/message-passing bridge between Bun and Zig cannot serve them — you need a synchronous FFI path, and each measure call must complete in microseconds because layout passes call it once per text node.

There is essentially no official host config documentation; the README explicitly disclaims API stability, so budget time for reading ink/react-three-fiber source and expect to re-verify the interface at every React upgrade.

Suspense fallbacks require hideInstance/unhideInstance to hide-without-unmounting; mapping this to native widget visibility is easy to forget and Suspense will appear to 'work' until a fallback leaves hidden widgets permanently invisible or double-visible.

Marketing-style claims about RN New Architecture performance (e.g. '43% faster cold start', '40x faster JS-native calls') come from third-party blogs, not Meta benchmarks — treat the architectural design as proven but the specific numbers as unverified.

research.topic: GTK4 backend on Linux in 2026: versions, zig-gobject bindings, threading, lists, CSS, accessibility/automation, Wayland, packaging
key_findings: Current stable is GTK 4.22, shipped with GNOME 50 on 2026-03-18; GTK 4.20 (Aug 2025) added CSS media queries (prefers-color-scheme, prefers-contrast, prefers-reduced-motion) and Vulkan renderer fixes, and 4.22's headline feature is GtkSvg, a native SVG renderer integrated with the GSK scene graph that supports SVG animations.

GTK's 2026 roadmap (FOSDEM planning) includes better accessibility, an Android backend, a C11 requirement bump, and a possible opt-in unstable-API channel; GTK 5 is not imminent, so targeting GTK 4.x (>=4.20) is safe for years.

libadwaita 1.9 (GNOME 50) adds AdwSidebar and AdwViewSwitcherSidebar and automatic reduced-motion, but it imposes the GNOME HIG design language; the GTK/libadwaita split exists precisely so cross-platform apps can stay on plain GTK4 general-purpose widgets, which is the right base for a framework mirroring AppKit/Windows widget sets.

GObject-Introspection GIR XML is the canonical machine-readable API description for GTK and the entire GNOME stack, making binding generation fully automatable; zig-gobject consumes GIR directly rather than hand-writing bindings.

ianprime0509/zig-gobject is alive and healthy: v0.3.1 released 2025-11-26, GNOME 49 profile support added Oct 2025, multiple-GIR-directory build support Jan 2026, and a 'feat: update to 0.16.0' commit merged 2026-04-20 (#152), so the master branch matches the host's Zig 0.16.0; bindings are zero-cost direct GIR translations with Zig idioms (camelCase methods, typed signal connection) and profiles track the latest two GNOME releases.

GTK4 is strictly single-threaded for UI: all widget/GDK calls must happen on the thread that owns the default GMainContext (the old gdk_threads API is gone); other threads hand work to the UI thread via g_idle_add or g_main_context_invoke_full, so the Bun/JS side must run on its own thread and marshal a batched mutation queue to the GTK thread per React commit.

Scalable lists use GtkListView/GtkGridView/GtkColumnView over a GListModel with a GtkListItemFactory that recycles row widgets (roughly 200 live widgets even for millions of items); GtkSignalListItemFactory's setup/bind/unbind/teardown callbacks map cleanly onto a React renderer's item-template mechanism, and the old GtkTreeView/cell-renderer stack is deprecated.

Runtime styling from user code works via GtkCssProvider + gtk_style_context_add_provider_for_display with priorities, and GTK CSS now has variables (var()), named colors, and media queries — but it is its own dialect: no display:flex/grid, no position, no flexbox properties; layout comes from widget containers (GtkBox, GtkGrid) and hexpand/vexpand, so the framework must map a style API onto widget properties plus GTK-CSS, not promise web CSS.

GTK4 replaced ATK with the built-in GtkAccessible interface (WAI-ARIA-like roles, states, properties, relations) exposed over the AT-SPI D-Bus bus on Linux; this accessibility tree is effectively the 'dump the live widget tree with stable IDs' layer for free, and tools like KDE's Selenium-AT-SPI/Appium already automate GTK4 apps this way, validating the approach.

In-process screenshots need no OS capture: a realized widget can be rendered to a GdkTexture via GtkWidgetPaintable/GtkSnapshot and the GSK renderer, then saved with gdk_texture_save_to_png — this sidesteps Wayland's screen-capture restrictions entirely and works headless.

Broadway (HTML5) and X11 backends were deprecated in GTK 4.17.4/4.18 and will be removed in GTK 5; X11 keeps working for GTK4's lifetime but gets no new features (no dmabuf, graphics offload, or Vulkan work), so the framework should be Wayland-first, and headless CI should run a headless Wayland compositor (weston --backend=headless or cage; GNOME 50's Mutter devkit also gained a simulator with virtual multi-monitor, HiDPI, and clipboard) rather than Broadway or Xvfb.

Wayland forbids global input injection (no XTest equivalent), so click/key synthesis must be in-process — synthesizing GdkEvents or calling widget actions directly in the automation layer — or go through libei/the RemoteDesktop portal; building synthesis into the framework core (like Playwright's in-browser dispatch) is both necessary and strictly more reliable than OS-level tools.

Flatpak packaging is straightforward: the GNOME 50 platform runtime ships GTK 4.22 + libadwaita 1.9, and the Bun runtime binary would be bundled as an app module (Flathub already has precedent for Bun-built apps); sandbox implications are that host file access and screen capture go through XDG portals, and the AT-SPI accessibility bus must be granted for out-of-process automation.

GTK 4.22 added an AT-SPI collection-interface wrapper API (requested by LibreOffice) for fast queries over large sparse accessibility trees — directly useful for a Playwright-style selector engine over big widget trees.
research.recommendation: Build the Linux backend on plain GTK 4 (require >=4.20, test against 4.22) using zig-gobject master, which already supports Zig 0.16.0 and generates bindings from GIR — the same GIR data can also drive the framework's own codegen for TS-facing widget metadata. Treat libadwaita as an optional add-on package, not a core dependency, since it locks apps into GNOME HIG. Architect the runtime with Bun on a separate thread and a batched mutation queue flushed to the GTK main thread via g_main_context_invoke_full (one idle dispatch per React commit, not per mutation). Implement the agent-first automation layer on GTK's own primitives: widget-tree dump and stable IDs via the GtkAccessible/AT-SPI tree (augmented with framework-assigned test IDs stored as widget data), screenshots via in-process GSK render-to-GdkTexture (Wayland-safe, headless-safe), input via in-process GdkEvent/action synthesis (Wayland has no global injection), and CI headless mode via a bundled headless Wayland compositor (weston headless or cage) — explicitly not Broadway or X11, both deprecated for removal in GTK 5.
gotchas: zig-gobject's tagged release v0.3.1 (Nov 2025) targets Zig 0.15; Zig 0.16.0 support only landed on master in April 2026, so pin a post-April master commit, and the binding generator needs xsltproc as a host dependency (fine in a Nix devshell, must be documented).

GTK CSS is not web CSS: no flexbox, grid, position, or display properties — LLM coding agents notoriously hallucinate web CSS here, so an agent-first framework should validate/lint styles against GTK's actual property set and surface parse errors loudly.
Broadway looks like an easy headless/screenshot path but is deprecated for removal in GTK 5 — do not build the CI story on it.
Wayland blocks both global screen capture and global input injection; any design that shells out to xdotool/scrot is a dead end — automation must be in-process or use libei/portals.

AT-SPI needs the accessibility bus (at-spi2 daemons) running; bare CI containers and Flatpak sandboxes need it launched/granted, or use GTK_A11Y=test which disables the D-Bus backend (fine for in-process tree walks, breaks out-of-process AT-SPI clients).
Widget-to-texture snapshotting only works on realized/mapped widgets, so even headless screenshots require a mapped window under a real (headless) compositor.

Per-mutation g_idle_add dispatch from the JS thread will destroy performance on large updates; batch each React commit into a single closure and beware that g_idle_add callbacks race with widget destruction (hold refs or use weak pointers).

Mixing libadwaita widgets into a plain-GTK app pulls in the Adwaita stylesheet and GNOME styling behavior (adw_init takes over theming), so the optional adwaita layer must be all-or-nothing per app, not per widget.

research.topic: AppKit backend from Zig on macOS in 2026: objc interop, Ghostty's architecture pattern, threading/layout rules, agent-first automation, and signing
key_findings: mitchellh/zig-objc is alive and production-proven (it is what Ghostty's Zig core uses for macOS-specific code): it wraps objc_msgSend with comptime-typed calls and supports class lookup/creation, dynamic method addition, protocols, blocks with captures, and autorelease pools; Zig 0.16 compatibility landed via PRs #31/#34 after Zig 0.16.0 shipped (April 2026), so it matches the host's Zig 0.16.0 today.

Ghostty's macOS structure is: libghostty, a C-ABI core in Zig (~93% of the repo), compiled to a static library and packaged with libtool + lipo + a module.modulemap into the GhosttyKit XCFramework, which a Swift app (AppKit + SwiftUI) links; Swift registers C callbacks in ghostty_runtime_config_s (wakeup_cb, action_cb, close_surface_cb, write_clipboard_cb) that the Zig core invokes, so neither side knows the other's internals.

Mitchell Hashimoto explicitly argues against writing the macOS GUI in pure Zig via the Objective-C runtime: Swift is where Apple is investing, several features are SwiftUI-only, and pure objc means 'fighting what Apple wants you to do'; he concedes the C-ABI-plus-Swift-shell pattern works best when the GUI layer is thin, which matches a React-renderer framework where the shell is mostly a widget factory driven by commands from the core.

Creating NSApplication/NSWindow/NSView from pure Zig is nonetheless proven feasible: colbyhall/objective-zig auto-generates Zig bindings for AppKit, Foundation, Metal and 30+ frameworks (with a working 1280x720 window example), but it is explicitly WIP with ~18 stars; zig-objc is the mature option but gives you raw msgSend ergonomics, so a pure-Zig AppKit backend means hand-writing every widget wrapper.

Swift-C interop is fully mature in both directions in 2026 (Zig exports C ABI for Swift; Swift exposes @_cdecl functions back to Zig), and Swift 6.2 added a safe C/C++ interop mode (std::span and friends) with Swift 6.3 (April 2026) extending C interop further -- but Swift-C++ interop is still officially 'actively evolving' and should not be a load-bearing dependency; plain C ABI is the stable boundary.

AppKit is strictly main-thread: NSWindow throws 'NSWindow should only be instantiated on the main thread!' and NSApplication.run must own the main thread; from Zig you can marshal work there without blocks via libdispatch's C API (dispatch_async_f onto dispatch_get_main_queue()), and Zig 0.16's new std.Io event-driven backend uses GCD on macOS, which composes cleanly with this model -- so the Bun/JS runtime and Zig reconciler must live off the main thread and post mutations to it.

For a custom cross-platform layout engine, use manual frames (setFrame), not Auto Layout: this is exactly what Yoga-based renderers do, and mixing your own computed frames with Auto Layout constraints causes conflicts; AppKit's default coordinate origin is bottom-left, so container views must override isFlipped to return true to get top-left/y-down semantics matching GTK and web layout.

Agent-first automation can be built entirely in-process without any TCC permission prompts: posting synthetic NSEvents to your own app via NSApplication.postEvent(_:atStart:) / sendEvent(_:) requires no Accessibility permission, and screenshotting your own views via NSView.cacheDisplay/bitmapImageRepForCachingDisplay requires no Screen Recording permission -- only cross-process automation (AXUIElement, CGEvent taps, ScreenCaptureKit) is TCC-gated.

Cross-process capture APIs changed: CGWindowListCreateImage is obsoleted as of macOS 15 in favor of ScreenCaptureKit's SCScreenshotManager, which requires the Screen Recording permission and silently returns window-less screenshots when unauthorized -- another reason the framework's screenshot facility should render in-process rather than capture the screen.

Every NSView/NSControl already implements the NSAccessibility protocol, and setAccessibilityIdentifier(_:) provides stable string IDs; a widget-tree dump with stable IDs can be generated either from the framework's own retained tree (preferred) or from the AX tree, and using standard AppKit widgets means external agents/screen readers get a usable AX tree for free.

True headless macOS does not exist: GUI apps need a logged-in window-server session, so CI runners (GitHub Actions macOS images, EC2 Mac) run tests headful in a logged-in session started via LaunchAgent; TCC permissions cannot be granted non-interactively without disabling SIP (tccutil TCC.db hacks) or MDM PPPC profiles -- which makes the in-process, TCC-free automation layer the only reliable CI story.

Distribution requires Developer ID signing plus notarization (notarytool; altool has been dead since Nov 2023), and macOS Sequoia (15) removed the Control-click Gatekeeper bypass -- unnotarized apps now force users through System Settings > Privacy & Security > 'Open Anyway' plus an admin password, a policy still in force on macOS 26 Tahoe -- so the framework's packaging tooling must automate sign + notarize + staple from day one.

SwiftUI as an escape hatch is cheap if and only if the macOS backend has a Swift shell: NSHostingView embeds SwiftUI views inside AppKit windows (Ghostty does exactly this for overlays like its command palette), whereas from pure Zig SwiftUI is effectively unreachable because it has no C ABI.

On ARM64, objc_msgSend must be cast to a concrete typed function pointer per call signature (no variadic dispatch); zig-objc handles this via comptime, which is the main thing you lose if you hand-roll raw objc runtime calls.
research.recommendation: Adopt the Ghostty pattern rather than pure-Zig objc for the widget layer: keep reconciliation, layout, and the Bun/TS bridge in a C-ABI Zig core, and implement the macOS widget host as a thin Swift/AppKit shell (built with SwiftPM/xcodebuild, linking the Zig core as a static lib or XCFramework) that exposes a flat C command/callback surface -- this mirrors the GTK4 C backend on Linux, keeps SwiftUI (NSHostingView) available as an escape hatch, and avoids betting on hand-written msgSend wrappers for hundreds of AppKit APIs; reserve zig-objc for small in-core needs (e.g. Metal, dispatch). Run NSApplication on the main thread with the Zig/Bun runtime on worker threads posting widget mutations via dispatch_async_f. Use manual setFrame layout with isFlipped container views driven by the shared layout engine, never Auto Layout. Build the automation layer in-process and TCC-free: synthesize input with NSApplication.postEvent, screenshot via NSView.cacheDisplay, and dump the framework's own retained widget tree with setAccessibilityIdentifier-backed stable IDs -- this is what makes agent-driven development and headful-but-permissionless CI actually work on macOS. Ship sign/notarize/staple automation (Developer ID + notarytool) in the CLI from the first release.
gotchas: zig-objc only supports released Zig versions, never nightlies -- pin the framework to Zig releases or carry patches.

Notarization requires the Hardened Runtime, which forbids writable-executable memory by default; embedding Bun/JavaScriptCore with JIT needs the com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit entitlement (and possibly disable-library-validation for native plugins), or JS performance falls back to interpreter mode.
isFlipped is not inherited by subviews -- every container view class in the widget tree must override it, or child coordinates silently invert.
SCScreenshotManager/ScreenCaptureKit fails silently (returns screenshots with no windows) when Screen Recording permission is missing, so never build the default screenshot path on it.
dispatch_sync onto the main queue from the main thread deadlocks instantly; the Zig-to-main-thread bridge must be async or check the current queue.

Cross-process AX automation has documented production failure modes on Sequoia/Tahoe: stale TCC caches after OS updates, kAXErrorCannotComplete from non-native apps, and kAXErrorAPIDisabled -- treat external AX as best-effort, not core.
Swift-C++ interop is officially still evolving and can break between Swift releases (real regressions filed against 6.2); keep the Zig<->Swift boundary plain C.

GitHub Actions macOS runners cannot grant TCC permissions non-interactively (SIP would have to be disabled), so any framework feature that depends on Accessibility or Screen Recording permission is untestable on stock CI.

research.topic: Native Windows UI from a Zig C-ABI core in 2026: Win32 vs WinUI 3/Windows App SDK vs Composition vs WebView2, Zig bindings, theming/DPI, and the automation layer
key_findings: Ranked option 1 for a Zig core: raw Win32 HWND windowing + comctl32 v6 where useful + Direct2D/DirectWrite custom-drawn widgets — every API involved is plain C or COM vtables, fully covered by zigwin32, needs no runtime redistributable, and matches how apps like Windows Terminal render their own content natively without XAML.

marlersoft/zigwin32 is actively maintained in 2026: commits on 2026-04-16 set minimum Zig to 0.14.0 and added Zig 0.16.0 support, a 2026-03-08 commit fixed COM struct-by-value return ABI (critical for Direct2D methods like GetSize), and bindings are regenerated from Microsoft's win32metadata (branch 23.0.2-preview as of April 2026), including COM interfaces for Direct2D, DirectWrite, DXGI, and UI Automation.

Windows App SDK is on a fast semantic-versioned train: 2.0.1 stable shipped 2026-04-29, 2.2.0 stable 2026-06-09, with 1.8.x still serviced (1.8.9, June 2026); 2.x added SystemBackdropElement (Mica/Acrylic anywhere in the tree) and TitleBar drag regions, and Build 2026 announced first-party DataGrid and charting controls.

At Build 2026 Microsoft dropped the 'WinUI 3' name in favor of just 'WinUI', publicly recommitted that no replacement framework is coming, and announced declarative (React/SwiftUI-style) C# UI support alongside XAML — WinUI is unambiguously the strategic native framework, but its projections remain C# and C++/WinRT only.

Calling WinUI from a non-.NET, non-C++ core is technically possible because WinRT is a COM-based ABI, but there is no supported C projection: a WinUI app must implement IXamlMetadataProvider and call the bootstrap (MddBootstrapInitialize in Microsoft.WindowsAppRuntime.Bootstrap.dll); Rust only achieves it through windows-rs's full winmd-driven WinRT projection (see the windows-reactor React-style crate), and Zig's equivalent generator (Vulfox/winmd-zig) is still a WIP — so WinUI-from-Zig is a large bindings project, not a weekend task.

XAML Islands are alive in Windows App SDK via DesktopWindowXamlSource/ContentIsland APIs (official islands samples show hosting WinUI content in a plain Win32 HWND app), giving a future hybrid path: Zig owns the HWND and message loop, WinUI content is embedded per-island — but it still drags in the CppWinRT/metadata-provider machinery.

Dark mode for classic Win32 common controls is STILL officially unsupported in Windows 11 as of 2026: it requires undocumented uxtheme.dll ordinals (SetPreferredAppMode ordinal 135, AllowDarkModeForWindow ordinal 133) plus the documented DWMWA_USE_IMMERSIVE_DARK_MODE DWM attribute; ozone10/win32-darkmodelib packages the technique (used by Notepad++), and WindowsAppSDK issue #5543 asking for an official API remains open — custom-drawn widgets sidestep this entirely.

UI Automation (UIA) is the built-in 'Playwright for native widgets' on Windows: a pure COM API (IUIAutomation client, IRawElementProviderSimple provider, UIAutomationCore.dll) where standard Win32 controls get providers free via OS proxies, custom-drawn widgets must implement providers, and the AutomationId property is exactly the stable-widget-ID mechanism the framework needs — all callable from Zig via zigwin32's ui.accessibility namespace, and it doubles as screen-reader accessibility.

Build 2026 directly validates the agent-first requirement: Microsoft shipped the winapp CLI plus generally-available 'Windows Development Skills' explicitly so AI agents (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) can scaffold, build, run, inspect, test, and package WinUI apps end-to-end without Visual Studio — a reference design worth mirroring and integrating with.

Flagship native apps in 2026: File Explorer and Notepad use WinUI/XAML islands inside Win32 shells (with a 2026 performance push), Windows Terminal is a thin Win32 window hosting WinUI 2 UWP XAML via XAML Islands plus its own DirectWrite-based text renderer, and the Files community file manager is C#/WinUI 3 — no flagship app builds its chrome from stock common controls anymore; the Windows-11 'native feel' comes from Fluent-styled custom rendering or XAML, not BUTTON/EDIT window classes.

DPI: the modern baseline is per-monitor-v2 awareness (DPI_AWARENESS_CONTEXT_PER_MONITOR_AWARE_V2 via application manifest or SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext), under which the app must handle WM_DPICHANGED and rescale; comctl32 v6 controls and non-client areas scale automatically under v2.

A useful middle layer without XAML: Windows.UI.Composition/DirectComposition can be driven from a plain Win32 window via the ICompositorDesktopInterop COM interface, giving GPU-composited visuals and animations for custom widgets from a C-ABI core.

WebView2 remains the mature HTML fallback and the natural embed point for a later CEF/browser-shell scenario (WinAppSDK 2.0 even improved WebView2 drag-out interop), but it is explicitly not a native-widget answer.

Zig cross-compiles to Windows via the MinGW target and zigwin32 needs no C headers at all, but MinGW headers are not C++/WinRT-compatible (ziglang/zig issue #23115), so consuming cppwinrt from zig cc is a dead end — WinRT access from Zig must go through generated COM vtable bindings.
research.recommendation: Build the Windows backend on raw Win32 windowing (zigwin32, min Zig 0.14 / 0.16 supported) with widgets custom-drawn via Direct2D/DirectWrite in a Fluent style — matching how the framework already plans to reimplement missing widgets — rather than binding WinUI: WinUI's WinRT ABI is COM and thus reachable from Zig in principle, but the lack of a C projection, the IXamlMetadataProvider/bootstrap requirements, and the immaturity of Zig WinRT generators make it a poor foundation in 2026 (keep it as a possible later backend once winmd-zig-class tooling matures, and use DesktopWindowXamlSource islands if individual WinUI controls are ever needed). Make every widget implement a UI Automation provider with a stable AutomationId from day one — that single investment yields the framework's mandatory agent/automation layer (tree dump, click/key synthesis targets, Playwright-style queries via IUIAutomation), OS-level agent interop (Microsoft's own Build 2026 agentic-Windows push rides on UIA), and screen-reader accessibility simultaneously. Use PrintWindow/Windows.Graphics.Capture for screenshots, per-monitor-v2 DPI from the start, the win32-darkmodelib ordinal technique (behind a version-checked feature flag) plus DWMWA_USE_IMMERSIVE_DARK_MODE for dark title bars, and WebView2 only as an embeddable content widget. Study and integrate with Microsoft's winapp CLI + Windows Development Skills as the reference for agent-first Windows tooling.
gotchas: zigwin32's README/docs still cite an ancient Zig 0.12-dev version, but the git history (April 2026) shows minimum Zig 0.14.0 with 0.16.0 support added — trust build.zig.zon and commit log, not the README.

Stock Win32 common controls render in Windows-8-era visuals and always in light mode; a 'native feeling' Windows 11 app in practice requires Fluent-styled custom drawing, so common controls are only useful for dialogs and scaffolding, not the widget set.

The dark-mode uxtheme ordinals (135/133) are undocumented and have changed semantics between Windows builds before (ordinal 135 changed from AllowDarkModeForApp to SetPreferredAppMode in 1903); gate them behind OS-build checks and design widgets to not depend on them.

Custom-drawn widgets get zero accessibility or automation for free — skipping UIA provider implementation per widget blinds both the framework's own agent layer and screen readers, and retrofitting providers later is far more expensive than building them in.

Windows has no true headless GUI mode: HWNDs need a window station/desktop, so CI must run in an interactive session (GitHub Actions Windows runners provide one) or a virtual/RDP session; capturing occluded or off-screen windows needs PrintWindow with PW_RENDERFULLCONTENT or Windows.Graphics.Capture, and this claim about CI runners should be validated with a smoke test early.

Any Windows App SDK/WinUI path adds a runtime deployment burden (WindowsAppRuntime framework package or self-contained payload) that raw Win32 does not have — relevant if WinUI is ever adopted as an optional backend.

Do not plan on using C++/WinRT headers from zig cc — Zig's MinGW-based Windows target cannot compile them (ziglang/zig #23115); any WinRT interop (Composition, Windows.Graphics.Capture, islands) must go through hand-written or generated COM vtable declarations in Zig.

win32metadata-generated bindings do not exactly match classic C headers (type normalization, A/W function mapping, non-null pointer annotations), so code ported from C samples needs mechanical adaptation and occasional workarounds for metadata bugs.

research.topic: Prior art autopsy (July 2026): desktop app frameworks relevant to a Zig+Bun, React-to-native-widgets framework with built-in agent automation
key_findings: Electrobun (blackboardsh/electrobun, ~12.5k stars) shipped v1 in early 2026 and is the direct proof that a Zig+Bun host works: Bun runs the main process and bundler, a native wrapper in Zig/ObjC/C++ owns windows/webviews, and apps land around 14-16MB using self-extracting ZSTD bundles with a Zig bsdiff updater that ships deltas as small as 4KB.

Electrobun's IPC model is concrete and copyable: one primary named pipe carries rpc-anywhere-encoded JSON between Bun and Zig (with a minimal Zig rpc-anywhere implementation offering a promise-like blocking API), a Zig-side listener thread uses kqueue-grouped pipe events instead of busy-waiting, and each webview gets its own named-pipe pair that Zig bridges opaquely without deserializing traffic.

Electrobun's biggest 2026 risk is instructive: Bun is rewriting its core from Zig to Rust (oven-sh PR #30412), and Electrobun has publicly not responded, showing that coupling a framework to Bun's internal Zig API is fragile — integrate with Bun at the process/FFI boundary instead; Electrobun is also effectively a single-maintainer project with narrow official OS support (macOS 14+, Windows 11+, Ubuntu 22.04+).

Tauri v2 is stable, security-audited, and the default 2026 recommendation for webview apps, but its single most common complaint — cross-platform webview inconsistency (WebView2 vs WebKit rendering/CSS quirks) — is the strongest argument for this project's no-webview premise.

React-NodeGui, the closest historical prior art (React renderer over Qt widgets from Node), is officially unmaintained with a 'fork it if you want it' notice, while the underlying NodeGui core is still alive (v0.74.2, May 2026, Qt6, Node 24, 9.2k stars, idle CPU ~0% and <20MB RAM) — the renderer layer died even though the binding layer survived, because hand-maintaining a React renderer plus hand-written widget bindings exceeded a single maintainer's capacity (macOS ARM support is still an open help-wanted issue).

Proton Native died for a precisely documented reason: it depended on the alpha-quality libui-node bindings it did not control, got flooded with 'add more components' requests it could not satisfy, pivoted to writing its own Qt bindings (node-qt-napi), and then the sole maintainer ran out of time — the lesson is that widget-breadth demand is what buries native-widget frameworks, so bindings must be code-generated from machine-readable metadata, never hand-written.

Yue/yue-node (zcbenz's C++ cross-platform native-widget library with Node bindings) proves one excellent engineer can build a working GTK/AppKit/Win32 widget abstraction, but its last release was v0.15.6 in January 2025 and it is effectively dormant — the same bus-factor-1 death pattern as Proton Native and React-NodeGui.

React Native Windows v0.82 (2026) is Fabric-only, and the critical architectural fact is that Microsoft's Fabric renderer draws via Windows Composition rather than a native XAML widget tree — XAML/WinUI controls are hosted only as opt-in islands via ContentIsland APIs — meaning the best-funded team ever to attempt React-driven native Windows widgets deliberately retreated to composition-plus-islands; react-native-macos remains maintained but chronically lags upstream React Native versions.

Flutter desktop was handed to Canonical as lead maintainer and 'strategic steward' at Google I/O 2026 after Google's post-2024-layoffs shift to maintenance mode; it draws its own pixels (not native widgets), and its trajectory shows even a giant backer treats cross-platform desktop as a cost center.

Socket Runtime is explicitly marked deprecated on GitHub (repo moved to heapwolf/socket, ~1.7k stars, no recent commits) — a cautionary tale of a VC-backed webview runtime dying; Wails v3 is still alpha in July 2026 after ~3 years (alpha2 released 2026-07-03, no stable date), showing cross-platform native windowing polish always takes longer than planned; Neutralino is alive and shipping (v6.7.0, GSoC 2026 org) in the ultra-light webview niche.

Slint (stable 1.x, dual-licensed company, Rust/C++/JS/Python APIs, compiles UI to machine code) and gpui (now a standalone Apache-2.0 crate on crates.io, with longbridge/gpui-component providing 60+ widgets) are healthy, but both render owned pixels — they are competitors for the 'fast non-web desktop UI' niche, not prior art for native widgets; the surviving Rust GUI ecosystem uniformly chose owned-pixel rendering over native widget trees.

GTKX (gtkx-org/gtkx, v0.21.0 March 2026, 316 stars, 1,082 commits, active) is the closest living prior art and validates this project's exact thesis on Linux: React/TSX drives real GTK4/libadwaita widgets via a custom react-reconciler, a Rust NAPI addon owns the single GLib main-loop thread, bindings are code-generated from GObject-Introspection (GIR) XML, and it ships @gtkx/testing (Testing Library-style), @gtkx/vitest (headless display isolation), and @gtkx/mcp (an MCP server exposing live widgets to AI agents) — proof that codegen'd bindings plus agent-first tooling is the modern playbook, but it is Linux-only.

Revery (ReasonML, owned-pixel) is dead with the ReasonML ecosystem; libui-ng survives as a minimal mid-alpha C library whose Node bindings (libui-node) have not been published in 8 years — the 'small portable C widget library' path repeatedly fails to reach usable widget breadth.

On the demand question: the graveyard (Proton Native ~11k stars, React-NodeGui, Yue) plus GTKX's traction shows persistent developer demand for 'React but real native widgets' that has never been killed by lack of interest — every death was an execution failure (hand-written bindings, alpha dependencies, bus-factor 1); the counter-evidence is that Microsoft (RNW) and Google (Flutter) both examined native widget trees with real money and chose composition/owned-pixel rendering instead, which flags Windows as the platform where a pure native-widget tree is most likely to break the team.
research.recommendation: Build it, but steal deliberately: copy Electrobun's proven process model (Bun main process talking to a Zig native host over named pipes with typed rpc-anywhere-style RPC, plus opaque per-view channels) while keeping Bun at arm's length (process boundary or stable FFI, never Bun's internal Zig API, because Bun's core is moving to Rust); make GTKX the design reference for the widget layer — code-generate all bindings from machine-readable metadata (GIR on Linux, ideally Apple's Swift/ObjC interface data on macOS and WinRT/WinUI metadata on Windows) because every hand-written-binding predecessor (Proton Native, React-NodeGui, Yue) died under widget-breadth demand; ship Linux/GTK4 first where headless CI (Xvfb/weston-headless), AT-SPI accessibility-tree dumping, and GIR make the agent-first automation layer (screenshot, input synthesis, widget-tree dump with stable IDs, MCP server) genuinely tractable and where GTKX has already proven the whole stack including AI-agent tooling; and treat Windows as the known hard case — Microsoft's own retreat from XAML widget trees to Composition-plus-islands says plan for a hybrid there (native widgets where they exist, composition-drawn or island-hosted fallbacks for the rest) rather than promising a pure native-widget tree on all three platforms. The differentiator nobody has shipped is exactly the combination of cross-platform native widgets plus a built-in Playwright-grade automation layer, so make automation a core protocol feature of the Zig host (every widget gets a stable ID in the reconciler, the RPC layer doubles as the automation transport) rather than a separate tool.
gotchas: Bun's Zig-to-Rust core rewrite (2026, PR #30412) means any deep Zig-level coupling to Bun is a time bomb; Electrobun itself has not yet answered this and is the canary to watch.

Do not cite React Native Windows as proof that React-driven native widgets works at scale — its Fabric renderer draws via Windows Composition and only hosts XAML as islands; it is actually evidence that Microsoft retreated from the native-widget-tree approach.

Marketing sites lie about maintenance: react.nodegui.org still says 'maintained by an active community' while the GitHub repo carries an unmaintained/fork-it notice — always verify status from repo commit history, not project websites.

The recurring death pattern is bus-factor 1 crushed by widget-breadth requests ('add more components'); hand-written bindings make this fatal, so binding codegen from GIR/WinMD/ObjC-metadata is a hard requirement, not an optimization.

Electrobun's 'written in Zig' branding overstates it: the repo is 34% TypeScript, 26% C++, 12.6% Zig, 9.4% ObjC++ — the native wrapper is a polyglot mix, and official platform support is narrow (macOS 14+, Windows 11+, Ubuntu 22.04+).

GTKX validates the architecture and the MCP/agent tooling but not the market: it is Linux-only, young (v0.21.0, 316 stars), and single-ecosystem (GNOME/libadwaita), so its existence proves feasibility, not demand at scale.

Wails v3 being still-alpha after ~3 years and Flutter desktop being handed off to Canonical are both timeline warnings: cross-platform native windowing and desktop platform upkeep reliably take multiples of the initial estimate.

Qt is a trap for this project despite being the most complete widget set: NodeGui survives on it but React-NodeGui still died, LGPL/commercial licensing complicates a plugin-friendly open-source framework, and Qt widgets are not the platform's real native widgets anyway.
