research.topic: JS<->native bridge and IPC architecture for a Bun-hosted React → native-widget desktop framework (2026)
key_findings: In-process FFI is 3-4 orders of magnitude cheaper than any IPC: Bun measured bun:ffi per-call overhead at ~2ns (6ns total vs a 4ns native C baseline) thanks to JIT-compiled per-function bindings, roughly 2-6x faster than N-API, while the fastest cross-process transport (shared-memory ring buffer) is ~270ns round-trip and unix sockets/named pipes are ~2-6us per message (Victor Anderssén benchmark, May 2026).

Bun 1.3.x has complete Node-API surface (every napi_* function implemented, per-module napi_env fixed in 1.3, recent releases made node-sdl ~100x faster), so a napi addon is the production-hardened binding path; bun:ffi is faster but Bun's docs still label it experimental with known bugs, so the Zig core should expose a plain C ABI bindable through either mechanism.

Electrobun (Bun + Zig, the closest prior art) originally spawned Zig as a separate process because 'GUI applications require the main thread of a process to run a blocking event loop', and used named pipes carrying rpc-anywhere-encoded JSON (one primary bun<->zig pipe plus a dedicated pipe pair per webview so Zig never double-deserializes routing).

Electrobun v1 (announced February 6, 2026) inverted that architecture: 'As Bun's FFI stabilized, I replaced most of the Zig FFI layer I'd written and leaned on Bun directly', with Bun using shared memory when spinning up workers — i.e. the ecosystem's own Bun+Zig project migrated from multi-process named-pipe JSON to in-process bun:ffi for exactly the workload this framework targets.

React Native Fabric proves the batching model: JSI gives JS direct synchronous access to a C++ shadow tree, the diff runs in C++, and each React commit yields an atomic list of mutations (createView/updateView/removeView/deleteView) applied to host views in one batch per frame — mutations never cross the boundary one-at-a-time, and RN 0.85 added cloneMultiple to batch style updates further.

Fabric's event model answers native->JS ordering/backpressure: events are queued with priorities (discrete vs continuous, guessed from platform gesture spans; onScroll always 'default' priority), continuous events are coalesced (latest wins), discrete events are never dropped, and a RuntimeScheduler can grant synchronous runtime access for discrete-event dispatch; a recent refactor removed one of three legacy event-queue levels.

Chromium's Mojo shows the multi-process cost floor: Mojo measured ~50% slower than Chromium's legacy IPC (30% more instructions, 47% more i-cache misses), best-case end-to-end latency is 10-20us, and typical latency is dominated by task-scheduling on the receiver thread rather than the transport itself — meaning a multi-process design needs dedicated reader threads plus shared memory to be predictable.

Serialization benchmarks make JSON the outlier: FlatBuffers deserializes at ~81ns/op vs Protobuf ~351ns/op (M1 Pro) and JSON ~1732ns/op (Go), but for an ops stream a schema compiler is unnecessary — a custom fixed-layout binary command buffer written into an ArrayBuffer whose pointer Zig reads directly (zero-copy via bun:ffi ptr()) is both simpler and faster than FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto, which pay off mainly for versioned persisted schemas.

bun:ffi JSCallback is the bridge's weak point for native->JS: callbacks invoked from threads other than the creating JS thread fail (oven-sh/bun issue #15925), the threadsafe:true option is experimental, incurs per-call cost, and currently only works reliably when the other thread runs JS (a Worker) — so native code must never call into JS directly from GUI/worker threads; events should be queued in native memory and drained from the JS side.

Single-process single-thread cooperative pumping is viable on Linux: GLib supports non-blocking iteration via g_main_context_iteration(ctx, FALSE), and the libuv guide documents interleaving two loops with UV_RUN_NOWAIT-style polling (Julia's Gtk4.jl ships exactly this libuv<->GLib integration), so Bun's main JS thread can own both the JS event loop and the GTK4 main context, guaranteeing all widget signals fire on the JS thread.

Fast Refresh works with custom renderers: react-refresh hooks into any renderer built on react-reconciler >= 0.22 (0.25+ recommended) via setRefreshHandler, provided the reconciler and react-refresh/runtime are bundled in the same chunk and registered before React code runs; combined with an in-process design where the native widget tree lives in the same long-lived process, JS hot reloads can preserve the live widget tree instead of rebuilding windows.

Crash isolation is the one genuine argument for multi-process: in-process FFI means any Zig/GTK bug takes down the JS runtime and vice versa, whereas Electrobun/Electron isolate webview/renderer crashes; the pragmatic middle ground is in-process for the trusted widget core, subprocess isolation only for untrusted plugins (Bun Workers or helper processes over the same C-ABI protocol), and CEF later brings its own multi-process model regardless.

For the 60fps budget the transport is not the bottleneck once batching exists: a frame budget of 16.6ms fits thousands of even 5us pipe messages, and Electrobun's pre-v1 per-message JSON encode/decode was the real cost — so the design priority order is (1) one boundary crossing per React commit, (2) binary encoding with interned strings, (3) in-process calls, (4) vsync-aligned application via GTK frame-clock tick callbacks (gtk_widget_add_tick_callback) so mutations land before layout/paint.

An in-process bridge also serves the agent-first requirement directly: the Zig core that applies the command buffer already owns a live widget tree keyed by the renderer's stable node IDs, so the Playwright-style automation server (tree dump, screenshot, synthetic input) can be implemented in the Zig core against those same IDs and exposed over a local socket with JSON — where human/agent-readable framing matters more than nanoseconds.
research.recommendation: Build an in-process bridge: compile the Zig core as a shared library with a plain C ABI, load it from Bun via bun:ffi (with a napi fallback binding for production hardening, since the C ABI supports both). Bun's main thread owns everything: the JS event loop cooperatively pumps the native toolkit (g_main_context_iteration(NULL, FALSE) on Linux, manual NSApp event pumping on macOS where AppKit demands the first thread — which is Bun's main thread in this model). JS->native mutations: the custom react-reconciler HostConfig accumulates mutations per React commit into a growable ArrayBuffer as a custom fixed-layout binary command buffer (opcode + node-ID + interned-string-table payload, Fabric-style createView/updateView/removeView/insertChild ops), then makes exactly one FFI call per commit — applyOps(ptr, len) — which Zig reads zero-copy and applies inside a GTK frame-clock tick callback for vsync alignment. Native->JS events: never use JSCallback from native threads; Zig appends events to a native SPSC ring buffer with sequence numbers and priority tags (discrete vs continuous), and the JS side drains it once per loop tick via a single FFI call, coalescing continuous events (scroll/motion keep-latest) and preserving discrete-event order — Fabric's proven model. Do NOT adopt Electrobun's pre-v1 named-pipe JSON design; Electrobun itself abandoned it for bun:ffi in v1 (Feb 2026). Accept the crash-isolation loss for the core (a widget-toolkit crash killing the app is the same failure mode native apps already have); isolate only untrusted plugins in Bun Workers/helper processes, and let CEF supply its own process model later. Hot reload: Bun HMR + react-refresh through react-reconciler's setRefreshHandler, with generation-tagged node IDs so reloads can either reconcile against or cleanly tear down the surviving native tree. Expose the agent automation layer (tree dump with the same stable node IDs, screenshots, synthetic input) from the Zig core over a local socket speaking JSON — it shares the widget registry with the bridge, making it first-class rather than bolted on.
gotchas: bun:ffi is still officially experimental in 2026 ('known bugs and limitations... should not be relied on in production' per Bun docs) — keep the C ABI napi-bindable so you can swap binding layers without touching Zig; Bun 1.3.x napi is complete and fast enough as a fallback.

JSCallback breaks when invoked from a thread other than its creating JS thread (oven-sh/bun #15925), and threadsafe callbacks currently only work well from Worker threads — the entire native->JS path must be pull-based (JS drains a native queue), never push-based callbacks from GUI threads.

Bun cannot be embedded as a library (no libbun), so 'in-process' necessarily means Bun is the host executable and the Zig core is a dylib — the Zig code never owns main(), which constrains AppKit: NSApplication must be pumped from Bun's main thread rather than via a blocking [NSApp run].

Blocking g_main_loop_run()/NSApp run would starve Bun's event loop; the cooperative pump must be non-blocking iteration integrated with Bun's tick, and Julia's Gtk4.jl notes this kind of loop integration can hurt multithreaded performance if done naively (busy-polling vs fd-based wakeup).

Per-mutation RPC with JSON dies well before 60fps with large trees — Electrobun's pre-v1 architecture needed per-webview named pipes just to avoid double JSON deserialization; batching one binary buffer per commit is the fix, not a faster JSON parser.

If any component does go multi-process, Mojo's data shows latency is dominated by receiver-side task scheduling (typical case far worse than the 10-20us best case), so budget for a dedicated reader thread plus shared-memory ring, not just a socket.

Fast Refresh silently fails with custom renderers if react-reconciler is old (<0.22) or if the reconciler and react-refresh/runtime land in different bundles/chunks — the runtime must register before any React code executes.
In-process hot reload leaks native widgets if node IDs from the old JS world dangle across reloads — generation-tag IDs and have the Zig core garbage-collect orphaned generations on reload.

research.topic: Agent-first UI automation and introspection for a Zig+TS native-widget desktop framework (state of the art, July 2026)
key_findings: The winning screenshot strategy is IN-PROCESS rendering, not OS capture: because the framework owns every widget tree, it can snapshot any window without permissions on all three platforms — GTK4 via GtkWidgetPaintable/gtk_widget_snapshot into a GskRenderNode then gsk_renderer_render_texture() to a GdkTexture and gdk_texture_save_to_png(); macOS via NSView.cacheDisplay(in:to:) into an NSBitmapImageRep (no TCC prompt for your own views); Windows via PrintWindow(hwnd, hdc, PW_RENDERFULLCONTENT) or WM_PRINT on your own HWND.

OS-level window capture is actively hostile in 2026: CGWindowListCreateImage is obsoleted (hard compile error) as of macOS 15 and its replacement ScreenCaptureKit triggers the TCC screen-recording prompt plus Sequoia's periodic re-confirmation nag and an orange menu-bar capture indicator; on Wayland the only sanctioned path is the interactive xdg-desktop-portal Screenshot/ScreenCast dialogs; only Windows (Windows.Graphics.Capture IGraphicsCaptureItemInterop::CreateForWindow, or PrintWindow) is prompt-free.

OS-level synthetic input on Wayland is still not dependable in 2026: libei + the RemoteDesktop portal's ConnectToEIS method works mainly on GNOME/Mutter with matched versions of mutter/libportal/xdg-desktop-portal, wlroots compositors still lack libei support (KDE has its own gaps), and every portal session requires an interactive user consent dialog — so the framework cannot rely on OS input injection on Linux.

GTK4 deliberately removed every synthetic-event path (GdkEvent structs are private, gdk_test_simulate_button/key are gone — GNOME/gtk issue #1488), so in-process input must be SEMANTIC: the automation layer should invoke widget behavior directly (emit ::clicked / gtk_widget_activate, set GtkEditable text, drive GtkAdjustment for scroll), which is exactly the model of Windows UIA InvokePattern and macOS AXPress actions.

On macOS and Windows, real OS-level input is still available as an optional 'true input' mode: SendInput() on Windows needs no permission, and CGEventPost() on macOS requires the Accessibility TCC grant (AXIsProcessTrusted); keep these as a secondary mode for end-to-end realism, with semantic dispatch as the default.

The widget-tree dump should be the framework's OWN protocol (stable IDs derived from the React element tree plus a developer-supplied testID prop), while ALSO mirroring into platform accessibility (AT-SPI2 on Linux, NSAccessibility on macOS, UIA on Windows) — native widgets give the platform a11y tree nearly free, and mirroring keeps screen readers and external tools like FlaUI working.

AccessKit (Rust, with C bindings usable from Zig) became the cross-platform a11y abstraction of record: GTK 4.18 (March 2025) merged an AccessKit backend that is now how GTK apps get accessibility on Windows and macOS (Linux still defaults to AT-SPI), and GNOME's push-based Wayland-native 'Newton' successor to AT-SPI is built on AccessKit but remains an unstandardized prototype in 2026 — useful specifically for the framework's custom-drawn 'missing widget' reimplementations.

The Playwright MCP model has won the agent-interaction pattern: a structured accessibility snapshot rendered as text with stable per-snapshot refs (e.g. ref=e42) that the agent clicks by reference instead of pixels — deterministic, cheap, no vision model needed; Windows-MCP (2M+ users via Claude Desktop Extensions, on PyPI as uvx windows-mcp) replicates exactly this over UIA for native Windows apps, validating the approach for native widgets.

External Windows automation tooling collapsed, confirming the need for a built-in layer: WinAppDriver is effectively dead (no release since v1.2.1 in Nov 2020, closed source, 1100+ open issues), Appium's windows driver depends on it, and the maintained alternatives are FlaUI v5.0 (Feb 2025, .NET UIA wrapper) and pywinauto — nothing Playwright-quality exists for native desktop, which is the gap this framework can fill.

Headless Linux CI is a solved problem for this architecture: GTK4 runs under Xvfb (X11 backend), weston --backend=headless (Wayland socket with no display), or the Broadway HTML5 backend (still shipped in GTK4 and re-enabled in Ubuntu/Debian packages), and with in-process snapshots plus semantic input no GPU or portal is needed (force GSK_RENDERER=cairo for software rendering).

macOS CI reinforces the in-process design: pre-seeding screen-recording permission by writing TCC.db via sqlite works on some GitHub Actions images (macos-13) but is blocked by SIP on others and on hardened machines (actions/runner-images #9529), whereas NSView-based in-process capture needs no TCC entry at all and runs fine in the runner's GUI session.

Anthropic's computer-use tool (beta header computer-use-2025-11-24, supported by Claude Sonnet 5 / Opus 4.x) remains a screenshot + XY-coordinate action loop, so the automation server should ALSO expose a raw screenshot-plus-coordinate-click/key/scroll surface (with correct HiDPI logical-to-pixel remapping) so generic computer-use agents work alongside the smarter ref-based semantic tools.

Recommended architecture: the automation server lives in the Zig core (compiled into every app, enabled via env var/flag like NATIVE_AUTOMATION=1, one server per app process) speaking JSON-RPC over a local WebSocket or stdio pipe — Playwright's proven shape of thin clients driving one wire protocol — with a first-party MCP wrapper exposing tools: getTree/snapshot (stable refs + roles + names + geometry), screenshot(window|node), click/type/scroll/setValue(ref), waitFor(condition), and an opt-in OS-input mode; the Zig side resolves refs to live widgets and executes semantic actions on the UI thread.
gotchas: In-process widget snapshots miss things a real screen capture shows: OS window decorations, GTK popovers/menus and macOS sheets that live on separate native surfaces, window shadows, and externally composited content (future CEF, video overlays) — the screenshot API must enumerate and composite per-surface, or document the difference.

Semantic action dispatch bypasses hit-testing and z-order, so an agent can 'click' a button a real user could not reach (covered by an overlay, zero opacity, off-screen); mitigate by hit-testing the ref's center coordinate against the live tree before dispatching and failing loudly, like Playwright's actionability checks.
Do not plan on injecting raw GdkEvents in GTK4 — the structs are private and the test-synthesis functions were removed; any design that assumes event-queue injection on Linux is dead on arrival.

Wayland fallbacks for true input are all conditional: libei needs matched mutter/portal versions and interactive consent, ydotool needs root/udev access to /dev/uinput, and wlroots virtual-input protocols only exist on wlroots compositors — none is universal enough to be a default.

Even ScreenCaptureKit triggers the macOS TCC prompt unless you go through SCContentSharingPicker, and Sequoia re-prompts users periodically (monthly nag) with a persistent orange menu-bar indicator — never make OS capture the default path on macOS.

PrintWindow with PW_RENDERFULLCONTENT requires Windows 8.1+ and DWM; some GPU-composited content (D3D swapchains, DirectComposition visuals) can come back black, so keep Windows.Graphics.Capture as the fallback for those windows.

Coordinate-space mismatch is the classic computer-use failure: screenshots are in physical pixels while widget geometry is in logical units, and Anthropic's API additionally downscales large screenshots — the protocol must state its coordinate space explicitly and remap on HiDPI or agents will click the wrong targets.

AT-SPI tree dumps in CI containers fail unless the a11y bus (at-spi2 registryd over D-Bus) is running — one more reason the framework's own tree-dump protocol, not AT-SPI, must be the primary introspection channel on Linux.
research.recommendation: Build the automation server into the Zig core from day one, as a per-process JSON-RPC service (local WebSocket + stdio) with a first-party MCP wrapper, and make its primary channel the framework's own widget-tree snapshot with stable refs (React tree path + testID prop), imitating Playwright MCP's ref-based text snapshots. Implement screenshots in-process per platform (GTK4 GskRenderNode→gsk_renderer_render_texture, AppKit NSView.cacheDisplay, Win32 PrintWindow/PW_RENDERFULLCONTENT) so no portal or TCC prompt is ever needed, and implement input as semantic action dispatch on the UI thread (activate/click signals, set editable text, drive adjustments) with actionability hit-tests before dispatch — with an opt-in 'real OS input' mode (SendInput / CGEventPost / libei where available) for end-to-end tests. Mirror the tree into platform accessibility (AT-SPI2, NSAccessibility, UIA natively; AccessKit's C bindings for custom-drawn widget reimplementations) so external tools and screen readers work. For CI: Xvfb or weston-headless with GSK_RENDERER=cairo on Linux, plain GUI sessions on macOS/Windows runners since the in-process design needs no permissions. Additionally expose a raw screenshot + coordinate click/key surface (with explicit HiDPI coordinate mapping) so generic Anthropic computer-use loops can drive apps without the semantic layer.

research.topic: Packaging, distribution, and security model for a Zig + Bun + native-widget desktop framework (2026)
key_findings: Single-binary via `bun build --compile` works today and cross-compiles to bun-linux-x64/arm64, bun-darwin-x64/arm64, and bun-windows-x64, with assets embeddable (Bun.embeddedFiles) and `--minify --bytecode` for startup, but the output floors at roughly 50-60MB on macOS/Linux and ~100MB on Windows because the whole Bun runtime is embedded (bun.com/docs/bundler/executables; community measurements of 51-57MB hello-worlds).

There is no libbun: embedding Bun as a C library in a Zig host is still an open feature request (oven-sh/bun issues #14252 and #12017), so the two viable architectures in 2026 are (a) the compiled Bun binary is the process entry point and loads the Zig native layer as a shared library via bun:ffi/N-API, or (b) a small Zig host executable spawns Bun as a sidecar process over IPC, which is exactly what Electrobun does.

Electrobun v1 (Bun main process + Zig native bindings) is the closest packaging precedent: ~12MB self-extracting bundles, auto-generated installers and update artifacts for macOS/Windows/Ubuntu, and differential updates via a SIMD+zstd-optimized Zig port of bsdiff producing patches as small as 14KB - but patches only apply from the immediately previous version, with full-download fallback.

macOS: notarization mandates the hardened runtime, and any embedded JS engine with JIT (Bun's JavaScriptCore) requires the com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit entitlement (hard requirement on Apple Silicon, apps crash initializing JSC without it) plus typically allow-unsigned-executable-memory; every nested Mach-O in the .app (Bun sidecar, Zig dylibs, plugin binaries) must be individually codesigned with those entitlements before `notarytool submit` and stapling.

Windows signing: Azure Trusted Signing was renamed Azure Artifact Signing and reached GA in early 2026, restricted to organizations in US/Canada/EU/UK and individual developers in US/Canada only, at $9.99/month for 5,000 signatures with daily-rotated 24-hour certificates - and it does NOT grant instant SmartScreen reputation (nor does EV anymore); reputation still accrues per-publisher over time.

Windows packaging: MSIX requires a CA-trusted certificate even for sideloading, so the pragmatic 2026 default for direct distribution remains a signed NSIS/EXE or MSI installer plus a winget manifest in the community repo; MSIX is mainly worth it for Microsoft Store submission where Microsoft re-signs the package.

Linux: Flatpak has become the default desktop distribution channel and integrates via XDG Desktop Portals (GTK4 transparently switches to portals when it detects a sandbox), which suits a GTK4-native framework well; AppImage remains the best format for CI artifacts and portable one-file testing builds, so shipping both (Flatpak for users, AppImage for nightlies) is the common pattern.

Auto-update reference designs: Tauri v2's updater enforces minisign/Ed25519 signature verification on every artifact and cannot be disabled (latest.json + signature fields); Sparkle 2 is the macOS standard (EdDSA + Apple code signing verification, sandbox-safe via XPC services, binary deltas, RSS appcast); Electrobun's zig-bsdiff shows delta updates are cheap to build directly into a Zig core rather than bolting on platform updaters.

Size expectations for positioning: Electron apps typically ship 80-150MB installed, minimal Tauri apps are a few MB (with lto, opt-level="s", strip, and Tauri 2.4's removeUnusedCommands that dead-code-eliminates commands not granted in the ACL), and a Bun-based framework sits in between - ~60MB uncompressed but ~12-40MB as a zstd/self-extracting download, which is honest to advertise as 'smaller than Electron, bigger than Tauri'.

Permission model reference: Tauri v2's capability/permission ACL is the best-in-class design to copy - JS-side code is untrusted by default, every IPC command must be explicitly granted per-window via capability files, plugin permissions are namespaced (`${plugin}:${permission}`), and the ACL doubles as a dead-code-elimination manifest; a TSX-drives-native-widgets framework has an even larger trusted surface than a webview, so a per-plugin command allowlist at the Zig IPC boundary is essential, not optional.

Untrusted plugin execution: the 2026 industry standard for sandboxed third-party plugins is WebAssembly via wasmtime (Extism as a ready-made host framework, Zed's WIT-component extension system as the proven editor-scale example); WASI gives capability-scoped filesystem access, but Zig-native plugins are inherently unsandboxed, so a two-tier model (WASM for third-party, native for first-party/audited) is the realistic split - note 2026 CVEs show even wasmtime sandbox escapes happen, so keep host functions minimal.

Supply chain is an active battlefield: the Shai-Hulud npm worm hit in waves (Sept 2025 original, Nov-Dec 2025 '2.0' compromising hundreds of packages in hours with GitHub Actions self-hosted-runner backdoors, and a May 2026 'Mini Shai-Hulud' resurgence with 170+ packages), all propagating through preinstall lifecycle scripts - directly relevant because desktop apps bundle whatever npm pulled in at build time.

Bun's package manager mitigates the main npm attack vector by default: lifecycle scripts (preinstall/postinstall) do not run unless a package is listed in trustedDependencies, which a framework CLI should preserve and document rather than weaken; combine with committed lockfiles, `bun audit`/provenance checks in CI, and a minimal-dependency core.

Sparkle 2 and Tauri's updater both demonstrate that update-artifact signing keys must be separate from platform code-signing identities (minisign/EdDSA keypair generated by the CLI, public key baked into the binary), which lets the framework verify updates identically on all three platforms regardless of OS signing infrastructure.
research.recommendation: Adopt an Electrobun-shaped distribution architecture, upgraded for native widgets: make `bun build --compile` (or a Zig host + Bun sidecar, whichever the runtime research picks) the single-binary story with app JS and assets embedded, and accept the ~60MB uncompressed / ~15-40MB compressed footprint as the honest positioning between Electron and Tauri. Build packaging into the framework CLI from day one: macOS .app with hardened runtime + allow-jit/allow-unsigned-executable-memory entitlements, deep-signing of all nested binaries, notarytool + stapling; Windows signed NSIS/EXE + winget manifest (document Azure Artifact Signing at $9.99/mo as the default cert path, with MSIX only for Store); Linux Flatpak manifest (portals-aware, since GTK4 handles this transparently) plus AppImage for CI/nightlies. Implement updates in the Zig core: minisign/Ed25519-verified manifests (non-disableable, Tauri-style) with zig-bsdiff+zstd delta patches (Electrobun-style), optionally emitting a Sparkle-compatible appcast on macOS. For the security model, copy Tauri v2's capability ACL at the Zig<->TS IPC boundary (per-window/per-plugin command allowlists, namespaced plugin permissions, ACL-driven dead-code elimination) and run untrusted third-party plugins in wasmtime/Extism WASM sandboxes while first-party plugins stay native. Keep Bun's default lifecycle-script blocking (trustedDependencies) intact and enforce lockfile + audit in the CLI's build path to blunt Shai-Hulud-class npm attacks.
gotchas: Bun cannot be embedded as a library (no libbun; oven-sh/bun#14252 still open), and a July 2026 regression (#30717) broke bun:ffi dlopen() of embedded native libraries in --compile output during Bun's internal Rust rewrite - pin Bun versions and test the ffi path in CI.

Without com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit, JavaScriptCore-based binaries crash on Apple Silicon under the hardened runtime; forgetting to sign nested sidecar/plugin binaries with the same entitlements is the most common notarization failure.

Azure Artifact Signing is geo-restricted (orgs US/CA/EU/UK, individuals US/CA only) and provides no instant SmartScreen trust - new publishers will still see 'Windows protected your PC' warnings until reputation accrues, regardless of cert type.
bsdiff-style delta updates only chain from the immediately previous version; users several versions behind need full-download fallback, so the update server must always host complete artifacts too.

Flatpak's sandbox constrains the framework's built-in automation layer: screenshots and input synthesis inside the sandbox must go through XDG portals (ScreenCast/RemoteDesktop with user consent), so the agent-first automation APIs need a portal backend on Linux, not raw X11/Wayland calls.
Tauri's 'few MB' size story will be quoted against you: a Bun-embedded framework cannot match it because the JS runtime alone is ~50MB+; do not promise Tauri-class sizes.
WASM sandboxing is only as strong as the host functions you expose - 2026 wasmtime CVEs included sandbox escapes, and overpermissive host APIs (arbitrary fs/exec) nullify the sandbox entirely.

npm preinstall scripts are the dominant supply-chain execution vector (all Shai-Hulud waves used them); if the framework CLI ever shells out to npm/yarn instead of Bun's script-blocking installer, it reopens that hole.

proposals.name: NativeDesktop (codename "Hotline") — in-process Zig core + Bun host, React-to-native-widgets, agent-first
proposals.summary: NativeDesktop is a single-process desktop framework where a Bun executable hosts the app's React/TypeScript code and loads a Zig 0.16 core as a plain C-ABI shared library via bun:ffi (with an N-API binding of the same ABI as the hardened fallback). The custom react-reconciler renderer (mutation mode, vendored react 19.2 + react-reconciler 0.33) serializes each React commit into one zero-copy binary command buffer that crosses the FFI boundary exactly once per frame, RN-Fabric-style; the Zig core owns the authoritative retained widget tree with stable node IDs and applies mutations vsync-aligned. Platform backends are real native widgets: GTK4 via zig-gobject on Linux, a thin Swift/AppKit shell behind a C surface on macOS (the Ghostty pattern), and Direct2D/DirectWrite Fluent-styled custom widgets over raw Win32 via zigwin32 on Windows. The agent-first automation layer is compiled into the Zig core itself — the same stable-ID retained tree powers Playwright-MCP-style ref-based tree snapshots, in-process permission-free screenshots, semantic input synthesis, and headless CI — making agent-driven build/test a first-class protocol feature rather than a bolted-on tool.
proposals.process_model: One process, no IPC on the hot path. Bun (pinned 1.3.13/1.3.14; Rust 1.4.x validated later behind the same C ABI) is the host executable because no libbun exists; the Zig core is a dylib it dlopens. Bun's main thread is the process main thread and owns BOTH loops cooperatively: the JS event loop plus a non-blocking native pump — g_main_context_iteration(ctx, FALSE) on Linux (the Gtk4.jl-proven pattern, fd-wakeup-integrated rather than busy-polled), manual NSApp event pumping on macOS (AppKit demands the first thread, which is exactly Bun's main thread in this topology), and PeekMessage draining on Windows. All widget mutation and all widget signals therefore happen on the JS thread — no cross-thread marshaling for UI work at all. Threads owned by the Zig core: (1) an automation-server thread handling the JSON-RPC socket, which reads the mutex-protected retained tree directly and can report/diagnose even when the JS thread is stalled (a deliberate agent-facing watchdog), marshaling actual widget actions onto the main thread; (2) std.Io.Threaded pool for core async work (file watching, update downloads), written against the std.Io parameter convention so std.Io.Evented is a drop-in later. Crash isolation: accepted loss for the trusted core — a toolkit crash killing the app is the failure mode native apps already have; untrusted third-party plugins run out-of-process/off-thread in wasmtime (Extism) sandboxes or Bun Workers, and a future CEF webview brings its own multi-process model without changing ours.
proposals.runtime_integration: The Zig core exports a deliberately tiny flat C ABI (~15 functions): nd_init(callbacks, config), nd_pump(max_us), nd_apply_ops(ptr, len), nd_drain_events(ptr, cap) -> len, nd_measure_text(node_id, constraints, out) (synchronous — measure callbacks and useLayoutEffect reads cannot be async), nd_snapshot_tree, nd_screenshot, nd_dispatch_action, nd_shutdown. Bun binds it two ways from one header: bun:ffi (dlopen + ptr(), ~2ns/call, the default fast path) and a compiled N-API addon exposing the identical functions (Bun's officially stable path; also keeps us Node-compatible and immune to bun:ffi's experimental-status bugs like JSCallback leaks #7582 and the --compile dlopen regression #30717 — CI tests both bindings every commit). JS->native: the reconciler writes a fixed-layout binary command buffer (opcode u8, node-ID u32, interned-string-table payload) into a growable ArrayBuffer; one nd_apply_ops call per React commit; Zig reads the buffer zero-copy via the raw pointer and applies ops inside a GTK frame-clock tick callback (gtk_widget_add_tick_callback) / CVDisplayLink-aligned drain / DWM-synced apply so mutations land before layout and paint. Native->JS: never JSCallback from native threads — Zig appends to an SPSC ring buffer with sequence numbers and priority tags (discrete: click/key, never dropped, order preserved; continuous: scroll/motion, coalesced keep-latest, Fabric's model), and JS drains it with one nd_drain_events call per loop tick, mapping priorities onto react-reconciler's DiscreteEventPriority/ContinuousEventPriority. No JSON, no per-property calls, no serialization framework — FlatBuffers/protobuf pay off for versioned persisted schemas, not an in-memory ops stream we control both ends of.
proposals.renderer_design: Built on react-reconciler 0.33.0 in MUTATION mode (GTK/AppKit/Win32 are mutable retained trees; persistent mode is a Fabric artifact of Yoga we don't need), with the exact react@19.2.x + react-reconciler pair VENDORED into the framework bundle exactly as react-three-fiber v9.5 and react-dom do — the host config breaks on React minors (the 19.1->19.2 'resolveUpdatePriority is not a function' incident), so app React versions never float against it. Render-phase host config methods (createInstance, appendInitialChild, finalizeInitialChildren) are side-effect-free: they build cheap JS node descriptors only, because concurrent rendering can invoke them for work-in-progress trees that are never committed — real native widgets are allocated exclusively at commit, so discarded renders leak nothing. At commitMutationEffects the renderer emits the batched op list (CREATE_NODE, SET_PROPS with own oldProps/newProps diffing since prepareUpdate is gone, INSERT_BEFORE, REMOVE, SET_TEXT) keyed by monotonically-assigned, generation-tagged u32 node IDs — generation tags let Bun HMR + react-refresh (wired through setRefreshHandler, reconciler and refresh runtime bundled in the same chunk) either reconcile against or cleanly GC the surviving native tree on hot reload, preserving live windows across edits. Suspense: hideInstance/unhideInstance map to gtk_widget_set_visible / NSView.isHidden / ShowWindow so fallbacks hide-without-unmounting; the resolveUpdatePriority/getCurrentUpdatePriority/setCurrentUpdatePriority family is implemented against the event ring's priority tags so startTransition works day one; getRootHostContext/getChildHostContext always return non-null sentinel objects (React 19 treats null as 'missing'). Text measurement is a synchronous nd_measure_text FFI call into Pango/NSLayoutManager/DirectWrite, microseconds per node, ink-style. React Compiler 1.0 ships enabled in the default app template — it is renderer-agnostic and directly cuts commit traffic across the FFI.
proposals.layout_and_widgets: The TS API exposes a curated widget abstraction (~40 core components: Window, Stack, Grid, ScrollView, Button, TextInput, Label, Checkbox, Select, Slider, List, Menu, Dialog...), each defined once in a machine-readable widget manifest that codegens the TS types, the reconciler prop tables, and the per-platform Zig glue — hand-written bindings are what killed Proton Native, React-NodeGui, and Yue, so codegen from metadata (GIR via zig-gobject on Linux, the manifest-driven Swift shell on macOS, win32metadata/zigwin32 + our manifest on Windows) is a hard requirement. Layout is delegated to native containers, not a ported Yoga: Stack/Grid map to GtkBox/GtkGrid with hexpand/vexpand on Linux and NSStackView/NSGridView on macOS; on Windows, where no native layout containers exist, the custom-drawn widget layer runs the framework's own small box-layout pass over manual frames — and that same layout code is the future Yoga-lite for custom-drawn widgets on all platforms. macOS containers that take manual frames override isFlipped (per-class, it does not inherit) for uniform top-left coordinates. Missing-widget strategy is three-tiered: (1) map to a real native widget where one exists; (2) custom-draw in the platform's native rendering stack — GtkDrawingArea/GskRenderNode, NSView draw(), Direct2D/DirectWrite (on Windows this tier IS the primary widget set, Fluent-styled, matching how Windows Terminal/Explorer actually work — Microsoft's own retreat from XAML trees to composition says don't promise pure native widgets there); (3) escape hatches: NSHostingView-embedded SwiftUI on macOS, DesktopWindowXamlSource islands on Windows, libadwaita as an optional all-or-nothing add-on package on Linux. Every custom-drawn widget implements accessibility at birth — AccessKit (C bindings, the same backend GTK 4.18+ uses on Win/mac) plus a UIA provider with AutomationId on Windows — retrofitting is fatal. Styling is an explicit constrained style API (spacing, colors, typography, borders, visibility) compiled to widget properties plus a validated GTK-CSS subset via GtkCssProvider; the compiler REJECTS web-CSS properties (flex, position, display) with loud errors, because LLM agents reliably hallucinate web CSS at GTK — the linter is an agent-correctness feature.
proposals.extensibility: Three plugin tiers behind one capability ACL copied from Tauri v2: every native command a plugin (or the app's own JS) can invoke is declared in per-window capability files with namespaced permissions (fs:read, shell:spawn, automation:input), enforced at the Zig FFI boundary, and doubling as a dead-code-elimination manifest for release builds. Tier 1, TS plugins: ordinary npm packages that can register components and commands; installed via Bun with lifecycle-script blocking (trustedDependencies) preserved, lockfile + bun audit enforced by the CLI (Shai-Hulud-class preinstall worms are the live threat). Tier 2, native Zig plugins (first-party/audited only): C-ABI dylibs loaded by the core that can register new widget types into the manifest/codegen pipeline — they get retained-tree nodes, automation refs, and a11y wiring for free; on macOS they must be deep-signed with the app's JIT entitlements. Tier 3, untrusted third-party: wasmtime/Extism WASM components with WASI capability-scoped host functions kept deliberately minimal (2026 wasmtime CVEs prove the sandbox is only as strong as the host surface). Future scripting: quickjs-ng (v0.15+, pure C, embeds trivially from Zig) reserved as an in-process plugin-scripting engine that needs no Bun. CEF-someday flexibility is structural: the widget tree already supports foreign-surface leaf widgets (a node that wraps an externally rendered native surface), so WebView2/WebKitGTK land as ordinary widgets first, and a later CEF backend plugs in as a foreign-surface provider with its own helper processes — the automation layer composites per-surface and marks foreign content in tree snapshots. Because the JS runtime touches the core only through the flat C ABI (bindable via bun:ffi, N-API, or any future engine's FFI), swapping or embedding a different JS runtime — including a JSC-in-Zig fallback if Bun 1.4.x goes sideways — never touches the core.
risks: Bun platform risk: 1.3.x is the dead-end Zig lineage and the 1.4 Rust rewrite is already shipping regressions (e.g. #30717 broke bun:ffi dlopen in --compile builds); mitigated by pinning 1.3.13/1.3.14, the N-API twin binding, and the engine-agnostic C ABI — but a forced runtime migration mid-project is plausible.

bun:ffi is officially experimental; if its bugs bite, the N-API fallback costs measurable per-call overhead — acceptable only because the design is one-call-per-commit, but it must stay that way under feature pressure.

Cooperative main-loop pumping (Bun tick interleaved with GTK/NSApp/PeekMessage) is the least-proven piece of the architecture, especially on macOS where nobody ships this at scale; a fallback to a Zig-host + Bun-sidecar topology (Electrobun's pre-v1 shape) must remain reachable, which the C-ABI boundary preserves.
react-reconciler breaks on React minor releases with no semver; vendoring contains it, but every React upgrade is a scheduled migration project with source-level re-verification against ink/r3f.
Zig churn: 0.17 (~Aug 2026) reworks the build system months after we adopt 0.16; pin the toolchain Ghostty/TigerBeetle-style, keep build.zig thin, budget one migration per release.

Windows is the known team-breaker: custom-drawn Fluent widgets + per-widget UIA providers + per-monitor-v2 DPI + undocumented dark-mode ordinals is a large sustained investment, and Microsoft's own RNW retreat to composition proves pure native widget trees fail there.
Widget-breadth demand is the historical killer of every predecessor; if the manifest/codegen pipeline is ever bypassed with hand-written bindings, the project inherits Proton Native's death spiral.

In-process means no crash isolation for the core, and macOS notarization requires allow-jit/allow-unsigned-executable-memory entitlements with deep-signing of every nested binary — packaging mistakes here are the top field-failure mode.

proposals.name: NativeDesktop
proposals.summary: NativeDesktop is a two-process desktop framework: a Zig host binary that owns the platform UI main loop and the authoritative native widget tree (GTK4 via zig-gobject on Linux, a thin Swift/AppKit shell over a C-ABI Zig core on macOS per the Ghostty pattern, raw Win32 + Direct2D-drawn Fluent widgets via zigwin32 on Windows), and a Bun child process running the React app on a vendored react-reconciler in mutation mode. The two talk over one boring, debuggable transport — length-prefixed JSON messages on a unix socket / named pipe, batched to exactly one mutation message per React commit — with a tiny synchronous side-channel reserved for measurement reads. The agent-first automation layer (widget-tree dump with stable IDs, in-process screenshots, semantic input synthesis, headless CI mode) lives entirely in the Zig host and shares the same widget registry as the renderer, so it works even when the JS side hangs, and is exposed as JSON-RPC over a local WebSocket plus a first-party MCP wrapper. Every widget binding is code-generated from machine-readable metadata (GIR, win32metadata, and the framework's own widget schema) because hand-written bindings are what killed Proton Native, React-NodeGui, and Yue.
proposals.process_model: Two processes per app. Process 1 is the Zig host executable: it owns main(), the process main thread, and the native UI loop — g_main_loop on Linux, NSApplication.run inside a thin Swift shell on macOS (mandatory: AppKit requires the first thread, and Bun exposes no run-loop pumping API), and the Win32 message pump on Windows. The host holds the authoritative retained widget tree keyed by stable node IDs, applies mutation batches on the UI thread (g_main_context_invoke_full / dispatch_async_f onto the main queue / PostMessage — one closure per React commit, never per mutation), and runs two auxiliary threads using std.Io.Threaded: a protocol reader thread for the Bun socket and the automation server thread. Process 2 is Bun 1.3.13 (pinned; validated later against 1.4.x Rust builds) spawned as a child with the socket path in its environment, running the React app and the reconciler. We deliberately do NOT use Bun.spawn's ipc option (Bun-to-Bun only) or bun:ffi as the core transport (officially experimental, JSCallback thread bugs #15925/#7582). Crash isolation is the payoff of this topology: a JS exception or hang leaves the host alive — windows stay up, the automation server keeps answering (an agent can screenshot the frozen app), and the host can restart the Bun child and re-mount against generation-tagged IDs. A native-toolkit crash kills the app, the same failure mode every native app already has. Untrusted plugins later get their own isolation (see extensibility); CEF, if ever added, brings its own process tree under the host, which this topology already accommodates.
proposals.runtime_integration: The boundary is a framed protocol, not linked code — non-negotiable given there is no libbun (oven-sh/bun #12017 still open) and Bun's core moved to Rust in May 2026, killing any Zig-source coupling. Transport: a unix domain socket on Linux/macOS, named pipe on Windows, carrying length-prefixed (u32 LE) UTF-8 JSON messages — "NDP" (NativeDesktop Protocol). Three message families: (1) host←runtime CommitBatch { commitId, generation, ops: [{op: create|append|insertBefore|remove|update|setText|hide|unhide, id, type?, props?}] } — exactly one per React commit; (2) host→runtime Event { seq, priority: discrete|continuous|default, nodeId, name, payload } — the host coalesces continuous events (scroll/motion keep-latest) and never drops discrete ones, Fabric's model; the Bun side drains them on its normal event loop; (3) control (windowCreate, appQuit, ping). JSON is a deliberate simplicity trade: batched-per-commit it is fast enough at 60fps for realistic trees (a frame budget fits thousands of 2-6us pipe messages; Electrobun's pre-v1 pain was per-message encode/decode, not batching), it is human/agent-greppable with NDP_TRACE=1 logging every frame, and a binary command buffer is a contained later optimization behind the same op list. Synchronous reads (text measurement, getBoundingRect for useLayoutEffect) use a second socket where the Bun side writes a request and blocks on fs.readSync(fd) until the host's UI thread answers — a ~10-50us round-trip we accept because native containers do the layout, so sync reads are rare by construction; the docs and lint flag them as slow-path. The whole boundary is engine-agnostic: anything that speaks NDP over a socket is a valid runtime, which is our hedge against Bun 1.4.x regressions and the door to a QuickJS or Node runtime later.
proposals.renderer_design: TS side: react-reconciler 0.33.0 in MUTATION mode (native toolkits are mutable retained trees; persistent mode buys nothing here), bundled together with react@19.2.x inside @nativedesktop/react exactly as react-three-fiber v9.5 does — app React versions never float against the reconciler, because 19.1→19.2 broke every unbundled renderer ('resolveUpdatePriority is not a function'). Render-phase host config methods (createInstance, appendInitialChild, finalizeInitialChildren) are side-effect-free and allocate only cheap JS descriptors with monotonically assigned node IDs tagged by a reload generation — concurrent React can render and discard work-in-progress trees, so real GTK/NSView/HWND widgets are created only at commit. Commit-phase methods append ops to the current batch; commitUpdate does its own oldProps/newProps diff (prepareUpdate is gone in React 19); getRootHostContext/getChildHostContext return non-null sentinel objects; hideInstance/unhideInstance map to gtk_widget_set_visible / NSView.isHidden / ShowWindow so Suspense fallbacks work; resolveUpdatePriority maps host event priorities (discrete=click/key, continuous=scroll/drag) to React lanes so startTransition works. resetAfterCommit flushes the batch as one CommitBatch message. Zig side: the host validates ops, instantiates platform widgets via the codegen'd binding layer, and applies the whole batch inside one UI-thread dispatch — on GTK inside a frame-clock tick callback (gtk_widget_add_tick_callback) for vsync alignment. The host's retained tree (id → widget handle, type, props, parent, children, testID) is the single source of truth shared by the mount logic and the automation server. Text measurement is a host-side service (Pango / NSAttributedString / DirectWrite) reached over the sync channel. React Compiler 1.0 ships enabled in the app template — it is renderer-agnostic and directly cuts commit traffic across the socket. Hot reload: Bun HMR + react-refresh registered through the reconciler's setRefreshHandler in the same bundle; on full reload the generation counter increments and the host garbage-collects orphaned-generation widgets.
proposals.layout_and_widgets: One widget schema, three backends. The framework defines its own machine-readable widget schema (~20 core widgets for v1: Window, Box, Grid, Label, Button, TextInput, TextArea, Checkbox, Radio, Select, Slider, ProgressBar, Image, ScrollView, ListView, TabView, Menu, Separator, Spinner, WebView-stub) from which we codegen TS types/JSX intrinsics, Zig prop-appliers, and docs — the schema is the contract; backends fill it in. Linux: plain GTK4 >=4.20 (tested on 4.22) through zig-gobject master (Zig 0.16.0 support landed April 2026; pin a post-April commit, vendor it); libadwaita is an optional all-or-nothing add-on package, never core. Lists map to GtkListView + GtkSignalListItemFactory with a React item-template component driving setup/bind/unbind. macOS: thin Swift/AppKit shell (SwiftPM) linking the Zig core as a static lib with a flat C command/callback surface — Ghostty's proven pattern; the shell is mostly a widget factory, and NSHostingView keeps SwiftUI reachable as an escape hatch; zig-objc is reserved for small in-core needs. Windows: raw Win32 HWND windowing via zigwin32 (Zig 0.16 supported) with widgets custom-drawn in Fluent style via Direct2D/DirectWrite — stock common controls are Windows-8-era and can't do dark mode officially, and WinUI has no C projection, so we follow Windows Terminal's approach; per-monitor-v2 DPI from day one, dark title bars via DWMWA_USE_IMMERSIVE_DARK_MODE plus the version-gated uxtheme ordinal technique. Layout is delegated to native containers (GtkBox/GtkGrid with hexpand/vexpand; NSStackView; a small Zig stack/grid layout for the custom-drawn Windows widgets) — no Yoga port; Box/Grid expose a constrained prop set (direction, spacing, padding, align, expand) that every backend can honor. Styling is an explicit non-web style prop (colors, fonts, padding, margins, borders) compiled to GtkCssProvider rules / AppKit appearance properties / Direct2D brushes, validated at commit against the schema so hallucinated web CSS (flex, position) fails loudly with a fix-it message — an agent-facing feature, since LLMs reliably hallucinate web CSS at GTK. Missing-widget strategy, in order: (1) composite it from schema primitives in TS (shipped in @nativedesktop/widgets); (2) custom-drawn in the Zig core with an AccessKit-backed accessibility node (AccessKit C bindings — the same crate GTK 4.18+ itself uses on Windows/macOS); (3) platform escape hatch: a typed extension op that lets a native plugin own a subtree (NSHostingView SwiftUI island, GTK custom widget, DesktopWindowXamlSource island on Windows if WinUI controls are ever needed). Never hand-write per-widget bindings outside the codegen pipeline — that is the documented death of every predecessor.
proposals.extensibility: Three plugin tiers, all crossing the same audited boundaries. (1) TS plugins: plain npm/Bun packages running inside the Bun process — components, hooks, data logic; no new machinery. The CLI keeps Bun's lifecycle-script blocking (trustedDependencies) and enforces lockfile + bun audit to blunt Shai-Hulud-class attacks. (2) First-party/audited native plugins: Zig (or any C-ABI) shared libraries loaded by the host, registering new widget types into the widget schema registry and new NDP commands; each ships a metadata manifest (commands, permissions, widget schema fragment) that feeds the codegen so TS types appear automatically. Every command a plugin exposes to JS is gated by a Tauri-v2-style capability ACL: JS is untrusted by default, capabilities are granted per-window in the app manifest, permissions are namespaced plugin:permission, and the ACL doubles as a dead-code-elimination list for host command dispatch. (3) Third-party/untrusted plugins: WASM components under wasmtime (Extism as host framework, Zed's extension system as the model), with deliberately minimal host functions — 2026 wasmtime CVEs show the host surface is the real sandbox boundary. CEF-someday flexibility falls out of the process model: because the host owns windows/HWNDs/NSViews and the runtime only speaks NDP, a browser view is just another widget type whose plugin embeds WebKitGTK/WKWebView/WebView2 today, and a CEF plugin later can spawn CEF's own process tree under the host without touching the renderer, protocol, or Bun. The engine-agnostic NDP boundary is itself extensibility insurance: if Bun 1.4.x (Rust) regresses, a Node or QuickJS runtime adapter is a contained project.
risks: react-reconciler breaks on React MINOR releases with no semver; mitigated by bundling react+reconciler into @nativedesktop/react (r3f pattern), but every React upgrade is a scheduled migration, not a version bump.

Bun 1.3.x is the end of the Zig lineage and 1.4.x is a fresh Rust rewrite; we pin 1.3.13/1.3.14 and depend only on process-level features (spawn, sockets, bundler), but a long 1.4 stabilization could strand us on an unmaintained runtime — the NDP boundary is the escape hatch and must stay engine-agnostic in practice, not just on paper.

Windows is the known hard case: custom-drawn Fluent widgets mean we pay per-widget drawing, theming, DPI, and UIA-provider cost that GTK/AppKit give free; Microsoft's own retreat (RNW renders via Composition, not XAML widgets) says budget 2-3x the other backends and ship Windows last.

Widget-breadth demand is the documented killer of every predecessor (Proton Native, React-NodeGui, Yue); codegen from the widget schema plus the composite/custom-drawn/escape-hatch ladder is the mitigation, but 'add more components' pressure is still the top project risk.

Synchronous measurement over IPC is ~10-50us per call versus sub-microsecond in-process; apps leaning hard on useLayoutEffect or per-node text measurement will hit a wall — native-container layout minimizes the need, but this is a real, documented limitation of the process-separated design.

Zig churn: 0.17 lands ~August 2026 with a build-system rework, and zig-gobject/zig-objc/zigwin32 lag releases by weeks-to-months; pin Zig 0.16.0 exactly (vendored toolchain, Ghostty/TigerBeetle pattern), vendor the binding generators, keep build.zig thin.

Flatpak sandboxing constrains the automation layer on Linux: in-process screenshots and semantic input still work, but anything reaching outside the sandbox (real OS input, cross-app capture) needs portals with interactive consent — document automation as in-process-first everywhere.

Per-commit JSON encoding could become the bottleneck for very large trees (10k+ node initial mounts); the schema-stable op list makes a binary command buffer a drop-in optimization, but until built, initial-mount performance of huge apps is a known soft spot.
